title: Consensus in Effective Model Inference for Disordered Ising Systems
summary: When independent learners are trained on data from the same disordered system, finite and noisy samples can lead them to different descriptions of the underlying physics. We quantify the reproducibility of such descriptions through consensus, the degree of agreement among independently trained models. In a teacher-student framework on the two-dimensional random-bond Ising model, an ensemble of students each infers a single uniform effective coupling from a finite set of equilibrium configurations drawn from one quenched bond realization. Aggregating the inferred couplings across students and realizations yields the consensus distribution, whose width quantifies the agreement among learners. The variance of this distribution separates exactly into a finite-sampling contribution, bounded below by inverse of Fisher information, and a quenched-disorder contribution. Sum of these two variance is minimized near critical region, so the consensus width has a minimum near the pseudocritical temperature that sharpens with increasing disorder. The two minima arise from different mechanisms: the sampling term inherits the critical peak of the Fisher information, while the disorder term is temperature-independent at leading order and acquires its critical minimum only at fourth order in the disorder strength, through the covariance between the linear and cubic responses to the bond disorder. Because the students fit a uniform coupling to a heterogeneous lattice, the inferred coupling also carries a misspecification bias that survives in the infinite-data limit. This bias displaces the minimum of the mean-squared error above the consensus minimum, so the temperature at which independent learners agree most closely is not the temperature at which their shared answer is most faithful.

AI.tldr: Independent learners trained on finite, noisy data from the same disordered system can converge to different physical descriptions. Using a teacher-student setup on the 2D random-bond Ising model, the authors show that consensus (agreement among learners) is quantified by the width of the inferred-coupling distribution, which decomposes into a Fisher-information-bounded sampling term and a quenched-disorder term, reaching a minimum near the pseudocritical temperature; crucially, maximum consensus does not coincide with maximum fidelity due to misspecification bias.
AI.motivation: Finite and noisy samples cause independently trained learners on the same disordered system to produce differing descriptions of the underlying physics. The paper aims to quantify the reproducibility of such learned descriptions via consensus, and to understand how finite sampling and quenched disorder jointly limit agreement among learners.
AI.method: A teacher-student framework on the two-dimensional random-bond Ising model is used. An ensemble of students each infers a single uniform effective coupling from a finite set of equilibrium configurations drawn from one quenched bond realization. Inferred couplings are aggregated across students and realizations to yield the consensus distribution. Its variance is analytically decomposed into a finite-sampling contribution, bounded below by the inverse Fisher information, and a quenched-disorder contribution, analyzed to leading and fourth order in disorder strength via covariances of linear and cubic bond-disorder responses. Misspecification bias from fitting a uniform coupling to a heterogeneous lattice is also characterized.
AI.result: The consensus distribution variance separates exactly into sampling and quenched-disorder terms; its sum is minimized near the critical region, producing a consensus-width minimum near the pseudocritical temperature that sharpens with increasing disorder. The sampling term inherits the critical peak of the Fisher information, whereas the disorder term is temperature-independent at leading order and acquires its critical minimum only at fourth order in disorder strength via the covariance between linear and cubic responses. Misspecification bias survives in the infinite-data limit and displaces the mean-squared-error minimum above the consensus minimum.
AI.conclusion: Consensus among independently trained learners is maximized near the pseudocritical temperature, with a sharpening minimum as disorder increases, driven by distinct sampling and disorder mechanisms. However, the temperature of closest agreement is not the temperature of greatest faithfulness: misspecification bias shifts the minimum of the mean-squared error to a higher temperature, so maximum consensus and maximum fidelity do not coincide.

title: Universal sampling of spin systems across quenched disorder
summary: Statistical physics extracts macroscopic laws by averaging over the many microscopic degrees of freedom of a system. Disordered systems demand a second and far harder average, one over the quenched randomness itself. The classic analytical routes, the replica and cavity methods, become uncontrolled outside mean-field or tree-like limits, and conventional numerical algorithms like parallel tempering require expensive, independent equilibration for every disorder realization. In this work, we introduce a universal neural variational framework that amortizes inference across the disorder ensemble, eliminating both the need for per-instance Markov chain equilibration and the cost of retraining instance-specific variational ansatzes. Built on an encoder-decoder Transformer architecture, after training once, it produces an explicit approximation to the Boltzmann distribution given previously unseen disorder realizations without further optimization. We validate this framework on 2D Edwards-Anderson models, and apply it to the random-bond Ising model, successfully capturing the Binder cumulant crossings near the Nishimori multicritical point. These results shift the object of variational inference from the single instance to the disorder ensemble, opening a route to frustrated many-body systems where instance-by-instance computation is prohibitive.

AI.tldr: A universal neural variational framework amortizes inference over the disorder ensemble, producing explicit Boltzmann-distribution approximations for unseen disorder realizations after a single training run, without per-instance equilibration or retraining.
AI.motivation: Disordered systems require averaging over quenched randomness in addition to microscopic degrees of freedom. Classic analytical methods (replica, cavity) become uncontrolled outside mean-field or tree-like limits, while numerical algorithms like parallel tempering need costly independent equilibration for each disorder realization.
AI.method: An encoder-decoder Transformer architecture that learns a variational ansatz across the disorder ensemble. Trained once, it maps a given disorder realization to an explicit approximation of the Boltzmann distribution at inference time with no further optimization.
AI.result: Validated on 2D Edwards-Anderson models and applied to the random-bond Ising model, successfully capturing the Binder cumulant crossings near the Nishimori multicritical point.
AI.conclusion: The work shifts the object of variational inference from the single instance to the disorder ensemble, opening a route to frustrated many-body systems where instance-by-instance computation is prohibitive.

title: Information-Theoretic Characterization of Macroscopic Chaos Emerging from the Chemical Master Equation
summary: Open chemical reaction networks exhibit stochastic concentration dynamics at finite system sizes, whereas their macroscopic limit is governed by deterministic rate equations that can display chaos. In this Letter, we show theoretically that a rate of information loss constructed from two-time mutual information recovers the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy in the deterministic limit. We verify this result through numerical simulations of a Markov jump process for a three-species system involving seven reactions.

AI.tldr: A rate of information loss built from two-time mutual information equals the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy in the deterministic (macroscopic) limit of open chemical reaction networks, verified numerically via a Markov jump process for a three-species, seven-reaction system.
AI.motivation: Open chemical reaction networks show stochastic concentration dynamics at finite system size, while their macroscopic limit is described by deterministic rate equations capable of exhibiting chaos. A bridge quantifying information loss across these two descriptions is needed.
AI.method: Theoretically construct a rate of information loss from two-time mutual information and relate it to the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy in the deterministic limit; verify with numerical simulations of a Markov jump process for a three-species system with seven reactions.
AI.result: The information-loss rate derived from two-time mutual information recovers the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy in the deterministic limit, confirmed by numerical simulations of the Markov jump process.
AI.conclusion: Two-time mutual information provides a consistent information-theoretic measure linking stochastic chemical kinetics to the chaotic deterministic dynamics of open chemical reaction networks.

title: Orientational order on non-orientable domains
summary: We study the statistical properties of passive and active many-body systems with orientational degrees of freedom on non-orientable domains. By rephrasing topological constraints as non-local symmetry relations on an orientable double-cover, we show that non-orientability eliminates global rotational soft modes without acting like an external field. In a passive XY model, this results in topological caging, where orientational fluctuations that exhibit conventional diffusive behavior on a torus saturate on a Klein bottle to a finite value that we compute exactly in the thermodynamic limit. In models of active self-propelled particles with orientational degrees of freedom, topological caging persists despite continuously changing interaction neighborhoods. In an active Ising spin model, non-orientability enforces the coexistence of ordered anti-parallel domains with vanishing global polar order, a state that is absent on orientable domains.

AI.tldr: Non-orientable domains (e.g., Klein bottle) eliminate global rotational soft modes in passive and active many-body systems by acting as a topological constraint rather than a field, producing topological caging and a distinctive mixed ordered state.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to understand how non-orientability—a global topological property of the underlying domain—affects the collective and statistical behavior of many-body systems with orientational degrees of freedom, both passive and active.
AI.method: Topological constraints are reformulated as non-local symmetry relations on an orientable double-cover. This framework is applied to a passive XY model, active self-propelled particle models with orientational degrees of freedom, and an active Ising spin model.
AI.result: In the passive XY model, orientational fluctuations that diffuse on a torus saturate on a Klein bottle to a finite value, which is computed exactly in the thermodynamic limit (topological caging). This caging persists in active self-propelled particle models despite continuously changing interaction neighborhoods. In the active Ising spin model, non-orientability enforces coexistence of ordered anti-parallel domains with vanishing global polar order.
AI.conclusion: Non-orientability suppresses global rotational soft modes without functioning as an external field, yielding robust topological caging and a mixed ordered state absent on orientable domains, with implications for orientational order in both passive and active matter.

title: Narrow-line magneto-optical trap of titanium atoms
summary: We realize narrow-linewidth magneto-optical traps of $^{46}$Ti, $^{48}$Ti and $^{50}$Ti atoms based on a 1040 nm-wavelength transition, cooling atoms to a minimum temperature in one dimension of $T_z=990(20)$ nK and a three-dimensional temperature of $T_\mathrm{3D}=1.28(7)$ $μ$K. Atoms are pre-cooled in a broad-line magneto-optical trap and then transferred with about 25% efficiency to the narrow-line trap. We operate the narrow-line trap in two stages over 85 ms. First, a single cooling beam, blue-detuned from the narrow-linewidth atomic resonance, optically pumps and traps the atoms on a two-dimensional surface where the Zeeman shift from the applied spherical quadrupole magnetic field brings the light nearly to resonance. Second, four additional beams, counter-propagating in the transverse directions, cool and compress the atoms in all dimensions. The high magnetic moment of the laser cooling state makes the dynamics of the narrow-line titanium trap similar to those of other magnetic atoms. We measure the lifetime of the excited state of the transition to be $τ=8.2(9)$ $μ$s, indicating a transition linewidth of $γ/2π=20(2)$ kHz, and also measure isotope shifts on the narrow-line transition. We use Stern-Gerlach separation on the ultracold Ti gas to measure the $m_J$-distribution in the narrow-line magneto-optical trap, finding over 98% of the atoms in the stretched spin state.

AI.tldr: Narrow-linewidth magneto-optical traps of three titanium isotopes ($^{46}$Ti, $^{48}$Ti, $^{50}$Ti) at 1040 nm are realized, reaching 990(20) nK in 1D and 1.28(7) µK in 3D, with >98% of atoms in the stretched spin state.
AI.motivation: Titanium is a promising species for ultracold physics (magnetic atoms, isotope shifts, precision measurements), but narrow-line cooling had not been demonstrated for Ti. A narrow-line trap would enable much lower temperatures than broad-line MOTs, so the authors set out to build and characterize such a trap for the Ti isotopes.
AI.method: Atoms are pre-cooled in a broad-line MOT and transferred (≈25% efficiency) to a narrow-line MOT operating on a 1040 nm transition. The narrow-line trap runs in two stages over 85 ms: (1) a single blue-detuned cooling beam on a two-dimensional surface where the spherical quadrupole Zeeman shift brings light near resonance, and (2) four additional transverse counter-propagating beams for 3D cooling and compression. Excited-state lifetime and isotope shifts are measured, and Stern-Gerlach separation is used to determine the m_J distribution.
AI.result: Minimum 1D temperature T_z = 990(20) nK and 3D temperature T_3D = 1.28(7) µK. Excited-state lifetime τ = 8.2(9) µs, corresponding to a transition linewidth γ/2π = 20(2) kHz. Isotope shifts of the narrow-line transition measured. Over 98% of atoms found in the stretched spin state.
AI.conclusion: Narrow-line magneto-optical trapping of Ti isotopes is demonstrated, achieving sub-µK temperatures and strong spin polarization. The high magnetic moment of the laser-cooling state makes the narrow-line Ti trap dynamics analogous to other magnetic atoms, establishing Ti as a viable species for ultracold and precision experiments.

title: Janus Dipoles: Fundamentals, Realizations, and Emerging Applications
summary: The Janus dipole - featuring orthogonally oriented electric and magnetic dipoles with a 90-degree phase difference - has emerged as a powerful paradigm for wave manipulation. Unlike traditional Huygens dipoles used for directional control, this unique configuration exhibits strongly asymmetric, face-selective near-field behavior while maintaining a quasi-isotropic far-field radiation pattern. These remarkable properties make the Janus dipole an essential platform for directional wave shaping, with wide-ranging applications in on-chip photonics, quantum interactions, and wireless power transfer. This review systematically traces the rapid development of the Janus dipole from its foundational theoretical inception to its diverse implementation platforms across optical, microwave, and acoustic frequencies. In this paper, we explore the governing principles, classify realization strategies into passive Janus dipoles, active Janus dipoles, and advanced near-field coupling control, and highlight emerging frontiers. By bridging foundational electrodynamics with advanced device engineering, this paper serves as an essential reference and roadmap for researchers designing next-generation, highly integrated, and compact wave-manipulation systems.

AI.tldr: A review of the Janus dipole-a configuration of orthogonal electric and magnetic dipoles with a 90-degree phase difference that offers face-selective near-field control with quasi-isotropic far-field radiation-tracing its theory, implementation platforms across optical, microwave, and acoustic regimes, and classifying realization strategies into passive, active, and advanced near-field coupling control.
AI.motivation: The Janus dipole provides wave-manipulation capabilities distinct from traditional Huygens dipoles: it achieves strongly asymmetric, face-selective near-field behavior while retaining a quasi-isotropic far-field radiation pattern. Its rapid development across multiple frequency regimes and its relevance to on-chip photonics, quantum interactions, and wireless power transfer motivate a systematic review that consolidates scattered progress and guides future design.
AI.method: A systematic literature review that traces the Janus dipole from its foundational theoretical inception to diverse implementation platforms at optical, microwave, and acoustic frequencies, exploring governing principles and classifying realization strategies into passive Janus dipoles, active Janus dipoles, and advanced near-field coupling control.
AI.result: The review organizes the field's development, clarifying the Janus dipole's governing mechanisms, categorizing its implementation approaches, identifying emerging research frontiers, and bridging foundational electrodynamics with advanced device engineering.
AI.conclusion: The Janus dipole is established as an essential platform for directional wave shaping and as a roadmap reference for researchers designing next-generation, highly integrated, and compact wave-manipulation systems.

title: Geometric Ginzburg-Landau theory of charge ordering and commensurability
summary: The concept of quantum geometry has recently led to reinvigorated insights in a wide range of fields including physical responses, superconductivity, and optical transitions, with effects most pronounced in systems with nearly flat dispersion. Here, we show that it plays an essential role in charge density wave formation (CDW) -- an important physical phenomenon that is responsible for driving various sharp changes in material transport properties including metal-insulator transitions. We derive an effective Ginzburg-Landau theory including uncharted contributions and, as a highlight, discover a general criterion for both CDW formation and commensurability transitions where underlying electron-phonon interactions manifest purely as electronic quantum geometric enhancements/suppressions. We benchmark our framework in a class of transition-metal dichalcogenides and resolve a longstanding puzzle where well-established purely kinetic CDW criteria fail in describing the correct ordering wavevector. Besides rendering robust criteria and fundamental insights that are immediately relevant to several experimental charge ordering systems, our theory can also be applied directly to other phonon-mediated phases such as superconductivity, and can be used as an important tool to explore the interplay between various such states. More generally, our framework provides a recipe for investigating the role of quantum geometry in phase transitions.

AI.tldr: Quantum geometry is shown to govern charge density wave formation and commensurability transitions, yielding a general criterion that resolves a longstanding puzzle in transition-metal dichalcogenides where purely kinetic criteria fail.
AI.motivation: Quantum geometry has recently reinvigorated understanding of physical responses, superconductivity, and optical transitions, with effects strongest in nearly flat dispersion systems. However, its role in charge density wave (CDW) formation—a phenomenon driving sharp changes in transport properties such as metal-insulator transitions—remained unexplored.
AI.method: The authors derive an effective Ginzburg-Landau theory that includes previously uncharted contributions, enabling identification of a general criterion for CDW formation and commensurability transitions in which electron-phonon interactions manifest purely as electronic quantum geometric enhancements or suppressions.
AI.result: The framework yields a general criterion for CDW formation and commensurability transitions, and benchmarks successfully in a class of transition-metal dichalcogenides, resolving a longstanding puzzle in which established purely kinetic CDW criteria fail to predict the correct ordering wavevector.
AI.conclusion: The theory provides robust criteria and fundamental insights relevant to experimental charge-ordering systems, extends directly to other phonon-mediated phases such as superconductivity, and offers a general recipe for investigating the role of quantum geometry in phase transitions.

title: A new generation of effective core potentials: Selected heavy 5d and 6p elements
comment: 18 pages, 14 figures, 3 tables. To be published in the Journal of Chemical Physics
summary: We expand the correlation-consistent effective core potentials (ccECPs) library by developing semi-local pseudopotentials and matching basis sets by heavy-elements from $5d$ (Hf, Os, Hg) and $6p$ (Tl, Po, At, Rn) blocks. In order to accurately capture scalar relativistic effects, spin-orbit coupling, and electron-electron correlation, we implement a tiered core-valence partitioning strategy across three distinct resolutions. This includes a small 60-core (Hf, Os, Hg) that explicitly correlates subvalence shells, a large 78-core definition for the main-group elements that rigorously accounts for core polarization and relaxation effects in sparse valence environments, and an intermediate 68-core partition for Hg and Tl. This 68-core architecture represents a unique development in the ccECP library, optimizing the balance between accuracy and computational efficiency in a manner unexplored for ligther elements. Optimized against relativistic all-electron CCSD(T) references, the ccECPs deliver outstanding atomic precision, achieving a global average atomic low-lying states deviation of just 0.045 eV. This accuracy translates directly to robust molecular transferability, systematically restricting dissociation energy discrepancies to under 0.03 eV, equilibrium bond lengths to within 0.005 Å. By enforcing a regularized, finite potential at the origin for enhanced numerical stability in stochastic quantum Monte Carlo methods, this library removes a critical methodological bottleneck for predictive many-body simulations of heavy-element systems and materials.

AI.tldr: The authors extend the ccECP library with semi-local pseudopotentials and matching basis sets for heavy 5d (Hf, Os, Hg) and 6p (Tl, Po, At, Rn) elements using tiered core-valence partitions (60-, 68-, 78-core), achieving 0.045 eV average atomic state deviation and sub-0.03 eV molecular transferability.
AI.motivation: Heavy-element systems lack accurate, transferable effective core potentials that simultaneously handle scalar relativistic effects, spin-orbit coupling, and electron correlation while remaining numerically stable for stochastic many-body methods such as quantum Monte Carlo.
AI.method: Semi-local pseudopotentials and matching basis sets were developed with a tiered core-valence partitioning strategy at three resolutions: a 60-core partition (Hf, Os, Hg) correlating subvalence shells, a 78-core partition for main-group elements capturing core polarization and relaxation, and a novel intermediate 68-core partition for Hg and Tl. Potentials were optimized against relativistic all-electron CCSD(T) references and regularized to a finite value at the origin.
AI.result: A global average atomic low-lying state deviation of 0.045 eV was obtained; molecular transferability yielded dissociation energy discrepancies below 0.03 eV and equilibrium bond lengths within 0.005 Å. The finite-at-origin regularization improves numerical stability for quantum Monte Carlo.
AI.conclusion: The expanded ccECP library provides accurate, transferable, and numerically stable pseudopotentials for heavy elements, removing a methodological bottleneck for predictive many-body simulations of heavy-element systems and materials.

title: Moiré Topology in Twisted Structures with Noncollinear Spin-Orbit Coupling
summary: Moiré superlattices provide a powerful platform for flat bands and correlated topological phases, yet most established examples rely on valley-contrasting Berry curvature in hexagonal lattices. Here, we propose a different route to achieve topological moiré minibands based on noncollinear spin orbit coupling in centrosymmetric type II SOC bilayers. Interlayer hybridization opens local pseudogaps and produces sharply localized Berry curvature, which twisting reconstructs into isolated topological minibands without requiring valley degrees of freedom or hexagonal symmetry. We demonstrate this mechanism in tetragonal Dresselhaus-SOC HgI2, where a Lieb-like moiré potential yields topological flat bands. To improve miniband isolation, we develop a physics-informed machine-learning surrogate that identifies stronger SOC as a key design principle and guides the replacement of Hg by Pb. The resulting PbI2 minibands are narrower and better isolated, supporting correlation-driven magnetism and tunable quantum spin Hall and Chern insulating phases, thereby providing an optimized material realization for experimental exploration.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a new route to topological moiré minibands using noncollinear spin-orbit coupling in centrosymmetric type-II SOC bilayers, demonstrated in tetragonal Dresselhaus-SOC HgI2 and optimized to PbI2 via a physics-informed machine-learning surrogate.
AI.motivation: Most established topological moiré platforms rely on valley-contrasting Berry curvature in hexagonal lattices, which constrains the design space. The authors seek an alternative mechanism that does not require valley degrees of freedom or hexagonal symmetry to realize isolated topological minibands.
AI.method: The authors exploit noncollinear spin-orbit coupling in centrosymmetric type-II SOC bilayers, where interlayer hybridization opens local pseudogaps and produces sharply localized Berry curvature that twisting reconstructs into isolated topological minibands. They demonstrate the mechanism in tetragonal Dresselhaus-SOC HgI2, where a Lieb-like moiré potential yields topological flat bands. To improve miniband isolation, they develop a physics-informed machine-learning surrogate that identifies stronger SOC as a key design principle and guides the substitution of Hg by Pb.
AI.result: The HgI2 system realizes topological flat bands via a Lieb-like moiré potential. Guided by the ML surrogate, PbI2 minibands are narrower and better isolated, and support correlation-driven magnetism as well as tunable quantum spin Hall and Chern insulating phases.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a valley-free, non-hexagonal route to topological moiré minibands and identifies PbI2 as an optimized material realization for experimental exploration of correlated topological phases.

title: Irrationality Measure Controls Long-Wavelength Charge Fluctuations in Quasiperiodic Systems
summary: Quasiperiodic order is characterized by irrational frequencies whose rational approximability known as irrationality measure defines distinct arithmetic classes. We establish that this arithmetic classification has direct physical consequences for long-wavelength charge fluctuations. In translation-covariant quasiperiodic systems, the infrared scaling of charge fluctuation is governed by the interplay between the irrationality exponent of irrational frequency and the large-harmonic decay of the hull charge profile: the latter determines the available charge weight, while the former controls how efficiently that weight is transferred to the infrared. Consequently, all algebraic irrational frequencies share the same arithmetic scaling, whereas exceptionally well-approximable transcendental frequencies can exhibit strongly enhanced infrared fluctuation scaling. We further prove that occupied states separated from the Fermi level by a gap stable throughout the hull contribute only an analytic infrared background, leaving the nontrivial scaling to near-Fermi states. Our results extend to general translation-covariant multi-frequency quasiperiodic systems.

AI.tldr: Distinct arithmetic classes of quasiperiodic order produce distinct long-wavelength charge-fluctuation scaling, with the irrationality exponent controlling infrared transfer and the hull charge profile setting the available weight.
AI.motivation: Quasiperiodic order is classified arithmetically by the irrationality measure of its frequencies, but it is unclear whether this purely number-theoretic classification has physical consequences. The paper asks whether arithmetic classes leave observable fingerprints on long-wavelength charge fluctuations.
AI.method: The work considers translation-covariant quasiperiodic systems and analyzes the infrared scaling of charge fluctuations, relating it to two ingredients: the irrationality exponent of the irrational frequency and the large-harmonic decay of the hull charge profile. It further examines gapped occupied states that remain stable across the hull, and generalizes the treatment to multi-frequency quasiperiodic systems.
AI.result: The infrared scaling of charge fluctuation is governed by the interplay between the irrationality exponent (which controls how efficiently charge weight is transferred to the infrared) and the large-harmonic decay of the hull charge profile (which fixes the available charge weight). All algebraic irrational frequencies share the same arithmetic scaling, while exceptionally well-approximable transcendental frequencies can show strongly enhanced infrared fluctuation scaling. Occupied states separated from the Fermi level by a hull-stable gap contribute only an analytic infrared background.
AI.conclusion: Arithmetic classification of quasiperiodic frequencies has direct physical consequences for long-wavelength charge fluctuations. Nontrivial scaling originates from near-Fermi states, while gapped states give only analytic background, and the framework extends to general translation-covariant multi-frequency quasiperiodic systems.

title: Generating is not discovering: a pre-registered physics judge for AI-proposed superconductors, calibrated on six known superconductors and one negative control
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures. Data, dated pre-registrations and supplementary tables S1-S7 at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22651560
summary: Generative models now propose millions of "stable" crystal structures, and their own referees have shown that stability is not discovery; no public benchmark asks whether a candidate has the physics to do a job. For superconductors the job is twofold: to pair, with a definite gap symmetry, and to become wire. We present a physics judge that answers both from a structure alone (DFT+U, a gated Wannier model, the full rank-4 RPA susceptibility on a $24^3$ mesh, the linearized gap equation, an irreducible-representation classifier, a manufacturability funnel) and measure what it says about what generators propose. With answer keys pre-registered before computing, the judge was calibrated on six known superconductors (Nb, Nb$_3$Sn, MgB$_2$, BaFe$_2$As$_2$, La$_{2-x}$Sr$_x$CuO$_4$, YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_7$), recovering the expected class in all six after two dated corrections. On the ruthenium analogue of the iron pnictide, with two runs and their criterion pre-registered the day before, it returns a null verdict at the same physical interaction where iron gives s$\pm$ ($λ_1 \le 0.0007$ versus 0.096; critical U 4.17 versus 0.97 eV); the pre-registered equal-alpha run fails the letter of the criterion, and we declare the resolution in favour of absolute U as post-hoc. The funnel reproduces the industrial map with thresholds fixed before running. Three generation audits follow: a descriptor sweep over 150 Materials Project metals re-finds the canon; 1,248 MatterGen structures yield 0 candidates that are new, stable and carry a pairing motif; mechanism filters over 47,893 compounds, validated by a blind hold-out, re-derive the community's analogies: geometry plus d-count is necessary but not sufficient. Generation re-finds what is known; judgment is the bottleneck. We propose a public benchmark over the eleven lists of AI-proposed superconductor candidates, none of which classifies gap symmetry.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a "physics judge" pipeline that, from a crystal structure alone, determines whether a candidate can superconduct (with a definite gap symmetry) and whether it is manufacturable into wire, then uses it to audit what generative crystal models actually propose. The verdict: generators re-find known chemistry, but physical judgment—not generation—is the bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Generative models now propose millions of allegedly "stable" crystal structures, but stability is not discovery: no public benchmark asks whether a candidate has the physics to perform a real function. For superconductors the function is twofold—electron pairing with a definite gap symmetry, and the ability to become a wire—and no existing benchmark classifies AI-proposed candidates by gap symmetry.
AI.method: A structure-only physics judge: DFT+U, a gated Wannier model, the full rank-4 RPA susceptibility on a 24^3 mesh, the linearized gap equation, an irreducible-representation classifier, and a manufacturability funnel. Calibrated on six known superconductors (Nb, Nb3Sn, MgB2, BaFe2As2, La2-xSrxCuO4, YBa2Cu3O7) with pre-registered answer keys and two dated corrections. Tested on the ruthenium analogue of the iron pnictide with the criterion pre-registered one day in advance (two runs), and applied to three generation audits: a descriptor sweep over 150 Materials Project metals, 1,248 MatterGen structures, and mechanism filters over 47,893 compounds validated by a blind hold-out.
AI.result: The judge recovered the expected gap-symmetry class in all six calibration superconductors after two dated corrections. On the Ru analogue it returned a null verdict at the same physical interaction where Fe gives s± (λ1 ≤ 0.0007 vs 0.096; critical U 4.17 vs 0.97 eV); the pre-registered equal-alpha run failed the letter of its criterion, and the authors declare the resolution in favor of absolute U as post-hoc. The manufacturability funnel reproduces the industrial map with thresholds fixed before running. The audits: the descriptor sweep re-finds the canon; 1,248 MatterGen structures yield 0 candidates that are new, stable, and carry a pairing motif; the mechanism filters, validated by blind hold-out, re-derive the community's analogies—geometry plus d-count is necessary but not sufficient.
AI.conclusion: Generation re-finds what is already known; judgment is the bottleneck. The authors propose a public benchmark over the eleven lists of AI-proposed superconductor candidates, none of which classifies gap symmetry.

title: Selected Coupled Cluster Guided by Selected Configuration Interaction
summary: Coupled Cluster (CC) theory is one of the most popular correlated wavefunction methods, yet the steep computational cost scaling of CC truncated at higher rank limits its application. Modern Selected Configuration Interaction (SCI) methods successfully exploit the sparsity of ground-state wavefunctions in the determinant space, motivating an analogous approach with the exponential CC ansatz. In this work, we introduce Selected Coupled Cluster (SCC), an arbitrary-order sparse CC method that explicitly solves the CC residual equations within a compact amplitude space guided by an SCI wavefunction. SCC optimizes the CC amplitudes in the sparse amplitude space. Using a pilot Just-in-Time (JIT) compiled implementation, we benchmark SCC against SCI, SCI+PT2, standard rank-truncated dense CC (CCSD, CCSDT), and DMRG across various chemical systems. We demonstrate that SCC exhibits fast, monotonic convergence with the SCI variational threshold, outperforming SCI and surpassing SCI+PT2 in the tight-threshold regime. SCC also provides accurate energies for high-dimensional topologies, where DMRG typically converges slowly with bond dimension. SCC thus presents an efficient drop-in enhancement for modern SCI workflows.

AI.tldr: SCC is an arbitrary-order sparse Coupled Cluster method that solves CC residual equations in a compact amplitude space guided by a Selected Configuration Interaction (SCI) wavefunction, achieving fast monotonic convergence and outperforming SCI/SCI+PT2 at tight thresholds.
AI.motivation: Coupled Cluster theory suffers from steep computational cost scaling at higher truncation ranks, limiting its applicability. Modern SCI methods exploit the sparsity of ground-state wavefunctions in determinant space, motivating an analogous sparse approach using the exponential CC ansatz.
AI.method: SCC explicitly solves the CC residual equations within a compact amplitude space guided by an SCI wavefunction, optimizing CC amplitudes in this sparse amplitude space. A pilot Just-in-Time (JIT) compiled implementation is used for benchmarking.
AI.result: Benchmarked against SCI, SCI+PT2, rank-truncated dense CC (CCSD, CCSDT), and DMRG across various chemical systems, SCC shows fast monotonic convergence with the SCI variational threshold, outperforming SCI and surpassing SCI+PT2 at tight thresholds. It also yields accurate energies for high-dimensional topologies where DMRG converges slowly with bond dimension.
AI.conclusion: SCC presents an efficient drop-in enhancement for modern SCI workflows.

title: Thermal Stability of Encapsulated Molecular Structures with Extended OH-Hydrogen-Bond Chains
summary: Using a coarse-grained model, we performed numerical simulations of the dynamics of linear molecular chains adsorbed on a flat substrate (on the surface of an h-BN crystal). It is shown that molecules containing benzene rings and hydroxyl groups in their structure can form stable hydrogen-bond chains OH$\cdots$OH$\cdots$OH. Such chains can be formed by phenol C$_6$H$_5$OH, 4-phenylphenol C$_6$H$_5$--C$_6$H$_4$OH, paracetamol CH$_3$C(O)NHC$_6$H$_4$OH, and 4-hydroxybenzanilide C$_6$H$_5$C(O)NHC$_6$H$_4$OH molecules. The dissociation of these chains occurs at temperatures above $T_1=190$, 240, 300, and 400K, respectively. Coating such molecular systems with a hexagonal boron nitride sheet (their van der Waals encapsulation) significantly enhances their thermal stability. Such encapsulated molecular structures retain hydrogen-bond chains up to temperatures of $T_2=470$, 800, 880, and 1140K, respectively. The simulations allow us to conclude that h-BN-encapsulated chains of these molecules can be used to create anhydrous proton-exchange membranes capable of operating at high temperatures. The most promising are encapsulated chains of paracetamol and 4-hydroxybenzanilide molecules.

AI.tldr: Coarse-grained simulations show that linear molecules with benzene rings and hydroxyl groups form stable OH···OH hydrogen-bond chains on h-BN; h-BN encapsulation markedly raises their dissociation temperatures, suggesting use in high-temperature anhydrous proton-exchange membranes.
AI.motivation: To identify molecular systems that can form thermally stable hydrogen-bond chains suitable for high-temperature anhydrous proton-exchange membranes. Hydrogen-bonded proton-conducting materials usually lose structural integrity above moderate temperatures, so a route to enhanced thermal stability is needed.
AI.method: Coarse-grained model and numerical simulations of the dynamics of linear molecular chains adsorbed on a flat h-BN crystal surface. Molecules studied: phenol, 4-phenylphenol, paracetamol, and 4-hydroxybenzanilide. Thermal stability assessed via dissociation temperatures T1 (free chains) and T2 (chains encapsulated by van der Waals coating with an h-BN sheet).
AI.result: Stable OH···OH···OH hydrogen-bond chains form in all four molecules. Dissociation temperatures T1 for free chains are 190, 240, 300, and 400 K, respectively. h-BN encapsulation significantly enhances thermal stability, with retained hydrogen-bond chains up to T2 = 470, 800, 880, and 1140 K, respectively.
AI.conclusion: h-BN-encapsulated hydrogen-bond chains of these molecules are promising for anhydrous proton-exchange membranes operating at high temperatures, with paracetamol and 4-hydroxybenzanilide being the most promising candidates.

title: Combinations of measurements that are simultaneous fits of parameters of interest and systematic uncertainties using the BLUE method
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables, submitted to EPJC
summary: Combining estimates of the same physics parameter obtained from different measurements improves the precision and robustness of the parameter determination. Modern particle physics measurements are often performed using likelihood fits that include the physics parameter(s) of interest together with nuisance parameters representing systematic uncertainties. In high-statistics analyses, typical of many analyses at the Large Hadron Collider, these nuisance parameters can be constrained in the likelihood fits. We describe how the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator method for combinations can be applied to both the estimates of the parameters of interest and the estimates of the nuisance parameters. We show with concrete example combinations that including the nuisance parameters can improve the precision on the parameters of interest. We show with pseudo-experiments that the uncertainty reported by the combination is reliable and that the approximate likelihood combination proposed in a previous publication and implemented in the Convino software reports an underestimated uncertainty. The method is implemented in an open-source software tool, Combiner.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE) method for combining physics measurements that incorporates both parameters of interest and nuisance parameters, implemented in the open-source tool Combiner, demonstrating improved precision and reliable uncertainty estimates.
AI.motivation: Combining estimates of the same physics parameter from different measurements improves precision and robustness. Modern particle physics measurements use likelihood fits with nuisance parameters for systematic uncertainties, and in high-statistics LHC analyses these nuisance parameters are constrained in the fits. There was a need to properly apply combination methods to both parameters of interest and nuisance parameters, and prior approximate likelihood combinations (e.g., Convino) reported underestimated uncertainties.
AI.method: The authors apply the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE) method for combinations to both the estimates of the parameters of interest and the estimates of the nuisance parameters. They demonstrate with concrete example combinations and validate uncertainty reliability using pseudo-experiments.
AI.result: Including nuisance parameters improves the precision on the parameters of interest. Pseudo-experiments confirm that the uncertainty reported by the combination is reliable, while the approximate likelihood combination from a previous publication (Convino) reports an underestimated uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: The BLUE-based combination method including nuisance parameters yields improved precision and reliable uncertainties. The method is implemented in an open-source software tool, Combiner.

title: Disordered ground states in one-dimensional exactly solvable fluids
summary: One-dimensional fluids of classical hard-core particles of diameter $a$, interacting in pairs via a soft repulsive (monotonically decreasing) potential of finite range $\varphi(x)=\varepsilon \left[ (a'-x)/(a'-a)\right]^{1/ν}$ $(a\le x\le a')$ with real positive parameters $\varepsilon$ and $ν$, are studied in an isothermal-isobaric ensemble. If $a'\le 2a$, the pairwise interactions are reduced to nearest-neighbour interactions, which allows for an exact solution of the thermal equilibrium. We focus on the $T\to 0$ ground states, specifically on the equation of state for the mean distance between nearest neighbours $l_0$ and the pair correlation function $g_0(x)$. If $\varphi(x)$ is concave $(ν\ge 1)$, there exists an ``incompressibility'' pressure $p_i=\varepsilon/(a'-a)$ such that the ground state is an equidistant chain of particles with spacing $l_0=a'$ for $0<p<p_i$ and with spacing $l_0=a$ for $p>p_i$. If $ν>1$ (strict concavity), the ground state at $p=p_i$ is disordered with $l_0=\left[ νa +(ν-1)a'\right]/(2ν-1)$ and $g_0(x)$ being a superposition of weighted Dirac delta functions over discrete positions. If $ν=1$ (linear ramp), the ground state at $p=p_i$ is disordered with $l_0=(a+a')/2$ and the continuous $g_0(x)$ is a superposition of Heaviside step functions multiplied by polynomials in $x$. The isothermal susceptibility at $T=0$ is nonzero for concave $\varphi(x)$ ($ν\ge 1$) at $p=p_i$ and, therefore, the corresponding disordered ground states are non-hyperuniform, i.e., they resemble disordered fluids at nonzero temperatures. It turns out that pair correlation functions of disordered ground states, which occur only at a single pressure $p_i$, extend their predictive power to thermodynamic states at nonzero temperatures over a wider range of pressures around $p_i$.

AI.tldr: The paper exactly solves the thermal equilibrium of 1D fluids of hard-core particles with finite-range soft repulsive pair interactions in the isothermal-isobaric ensemble, focusing on T→0 ground states and their pair correlation functions.
AI.motivation: One-dimensional fluids with soft repulsive finite-range potentials are tractable models that allow exact solutions, offering insight into ground-state structure, disorder at zero temperature, and hyperuniformity, with predictive value extending to nonzero temperatures.
AI.method: Study classical hard-core particles of diameter a interacting via φ(x)=ε[(a'−x)/(a'−a)]^{1/ν} for a≤x≤a'. When a'≤2a, interactions reduce to nearest-neighbour ones, enabling exact solution in the isothermal-isobaric ensemble; analyze T→0 equation of state for mean nearest-neighbour distance l0 and pair correlation g0(x), plus isothermal susceptibility.
AI.result: For concave φ (ν≥1) there is an incompressibility pressure p_i=ε/(a'−a) with equidistant ground-state chains: spacing l0=a' for 0<p<p_i and l0=a for p>p_i. For ν>1 the state at p_i is disordered with l0=[νa+(ν−1)a']/(2ν−1) and g0(x) a superposition of weighted Dirac deltas. For ν=1 the state at p_i is disordered with l0=(a+a')/2 and continuous g0(x) a superposition of Heaviside step functions times polynomials. The isothermal susceptibility at T=0 is nonzero for ν≥1 at p=p_i, so these disordered ground states are non-hyperuniform, resembling disordered fluids at nonzero temperature. The pair correlation functions of disordered ground states, occurring only at a single p_i, extend their predictive power to nonzero-temperature thermodynamic states over a wider pressure range around p_i.
AI.conclusion: Concave soft repulsive potentials yield an incompressibility pressure separating ordered equidistant chains; at p_i strict concavity produces non-hyperuniform disordered ground states with delta-function or continuous step-function pair correlations whose predictive power extends to nonzero temperatures near p_i.

title: Delay-engineered dynamical phases in a programmable non-Markovian spin oscillator
summary: Non-Markovian dynamics offer a new route towards engineering non-equilibrium matter, where memory and feedback act as programmable resources for controlling order in time. Here we report the realization of a non-Markovian spin oscillator in a hot vapour $^{129}$Xe-Cs co-magnetometer with programmable feedback delay and gain. By tuning these parameters, we observe a hierarchy of dynamical phases, including time-crystalline response, nonlinear bifurcations, and frequency-comb formation. The measured spectra and phase boundaries are captured by linear stability analysis of delayed Bloch equations, revealing these phenomena as different manifestations of the same memory-induced instability structure. These results establish time-delayed feedback as a powerful strategy for controlling non-equilibrium phases, enabling quantum sensing, frequency referencing, and synchronization within a single spin-based platform.

AI.tldr: The paper realizes a non-Markovian spin oscillator in a hot vapour 129Xe-Cs co-magnetometer with programmable feedback delay and gain, observing a hierarchy of dynamical phases (time-crystalline response, nonlinear bifurcations, frequency-comb formation) unified by a memory-induced instability structure described by linear stability analysis of delayed Bloch equations.
AI.motivation: Non-Markovian dynamics provide a route to engineer non-equilibrium matter, with memory and feedback serving as programmable resources to control order in time. The authors aim to exploit time-delayed feedback as a strategy for controlling non-equilibrium phases within a spin-based platform.
AI.method: A non-Markovian spin oscillator is implemented in a hot vapour 129Xe-Cs co-magnetometer with programmable feedback delay and gain. The observed spectra and phase boundaries are modeled via linear stability analysis of delayed Bloch equations.
AI.result: By tuning feedback delay and gain, the authors observe a hierarchy of dynamical phases: time-crystalline response, nonlinear bifurcations, and frequency-comb formation. The measured spectra and phase boundaries agree with the linear stability analysis, showing these phenomena arise from a single memory-induced instability structure.
AI.conclusion: Time-delayed feedback is established as a powerful strategy for controlling non-equilibrium phases, enabling quantum sensing, frequency referencing, and synchronization within a single spin-based platform.

title: Scattering-robust Imaging of Azimuthal Features with Enhanced Resolution
summary: Imaging through scattering media remains a long-standing challenge in numerous real-world applications, ranging from medical imaging to long-distance sensing. Recently, illumination consisting of a single orbital angular momentum (OAM) mode, which is structured in the azimuthal coordinate, has been shown to provide enhanced resolution for imaging objects with azimuthal features, with the resolution becoming maximum at an optimal OAM value. However, in the presence of scattering, single-mode fields, which are spatially fully coherent, cause the imaging resolution to decrease significantly due to speckle formation. In this work, we employ azimuthally partially coherent fields and experimentally demonstrate imaging of azimuthal features with enhanced resolution in the presence of scattering. We show that lower degree of azimuthal coherence in such illumination leads to increased robustness against scattering while the azimuthal structure of the illumination ensures enhanced resolution. We derive the condition for best imaging resolution, and we report increase of imaging contrast in scattering from about 7% to 50% as the illumination is changed from a single-mode fully coherent field to that of an azimuthal partially coherent field.

AI.tldr: Azimuthally partially coherent fields enable enhanced-resolution imaging of azimuthal features through scattering media, outperforming single-OAM-mode fully coherent illumination.
AI.motivation: Imaging through scattering media is a persistent challenge in applications like medical imaging and long-distance sensing. Single OAM-mode illumination improves resolution of azimuthal features but its full spatial coherence causes severe resolution loss under scattering due to speckle formation.
AI.method: The authors employ azimuthally partially coherent fields and experimentally demonstrate imaging of azimuthal features in the presence of scattering. They derive the condition for optimal imaging resolution and analyze the effect of reducing the degree of azimuthal coherence.
AI.result: Lower azimuthal coherence increases robustness against scattering while the azimuthal structure preserves enhanced resolution. Imaging contrast in scattering improves from about 7% (single-mode fully coherent field) to 50% (azimuthal partially coherent field).
AI.conclusion: Azimuthally partially coherent illumination offers a route to enhanced-resolution imaging of azimuthal features through scattering media, with a derived optimal-resolution condition and substantially improved contrast.

title: Lattice 2-group symmetries: operators, defects, and gauging
summary: We construct and study lattice realizations of finite 2-group symmetries in ${2+1}$d quantum lattice systems with finite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert spaces. We focus on two broad classes of 2-groups with 0-form symmetry group $G$ and 1-form symmetry group $A$: split 2-groups with trivial Postnikov class ${[β]\in\mathcal{H}^3(G,A)}$, and central 2-groups with trivial action ${ρ\colon G\to\text{Aut}(A)}$. In both cases, we construct symmetry operators on the full tensor-product Hilbert space that become 2-group symmetry operators when restricted to the topological subspace of the lattice $A$ 1-form symmetry. While the lattice split 2-group symmetry operators are onsite, the lattice central 2-group symmetry operators are not, and can only be made onsite after introducing ancillae. We extensively explore various manifestations of $ρ$ and $[β]$ for these lattice 2-group symmetry operators and demonstrate their agreement with expectations from quantum field theory. These manifestations arise in the transformation of operators carrying symmetry charge, the structure of lattice 2-group symmetry defects, and the dual fusion 2-category symmetries obtained by gauging the lattice 2-group symmetries. We further propose families of local symmetric Hamiltonians for both classes of lattice 2-group symmetries and identify exactly solvable limits lying in phases with spontaneous 2-group symmetry breaking and nontrivial symmetry-enriched topological order. In one such limit, the gauged Hamiltonians are exactly solvable lattice realizations of the corresponding 2-group gauge theories, whose ground-state degeneracies we calculate.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs and analyzes lattice realizations of finite 2-group symmetries in (2+1)d quantum lattice systems, covering split 2-groups (trivial Postnikov class) and central 2-groups (trivial action), and studies their symmetry operators, defects, gauging, Hamiltonian realizations, and emergent phases.
AI.motivation: Finite 2-group symmetries are well understood in quantum field theory, but their explicit lattice realizations in finite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert spaces remain underdeveloped. A concrete lattice formulation is needed to bridge QFT expectations with microscopic models and to enable the study of symmetry-breaking and symmetry-enriched phases.
AI.method: The authors construct symmetry operators for two classes of 2-groups: split 2-groups with trivial Postnikov class [β]∈H³(G,A), and central 2-groups with trivial action ρ:G→Aut(A). They build operators on the full tensor-product Hilbert space that reduce to genuine 2-group symmetry operators on the topological subspace of the A 1-form symmetry, using ancillae when needed to make central 2-group operators onsite. They analyze operator transformations, lattice 2-group symmetry defects, and the dual fusion 2-category symmetries obtained by gauging. They also propose local symmetric Hamiltonians and identify exactly solvable limits with spontaneous symmetry breaking and nontrivial symmetry-enriched topological order.
AI.result: The lattice constructions reproduce QFT expectations for the manifestations of ρ and [β], including the transformation of symmetry-charged operators, the structure of 2-group symmetry defects, and dual fusion 2-category symmetries from gauging. The proposed Hamiltonians admit exactly solvable limits in phases of spontaneous 2-group symmetry breaking and nontrivial symmetry-enriched topological order. In one limit, the gauged Hamiltonians realize the corresponding 2-group gauge theories, with ground-state degeneracies computed.
AI.conclusion: The work provides explicit lattice realizations of finite 2-group symmetries in (2+1)d, confirms consistency with QFT expectations, and offers exactly solvable Hamiltonian frameworks for studying spontaneous 2-group symmetry breaking, symmetry-enriched topological order, and 2-group gauge theories.

title: A Geometrically Parameterized Quasi-Stationary 3D Model for High-Frequency Induction Tube Welding
summary: A three-dimensional multiphysics finite element framework for the simulation of high-frequency induction welding of tubes is presented. The model couples a time-harmonic magnetic scalar potential formulation with a stabilized quasi-stationary advection-diffusion heat transport equation, enabling accurate prediction of electromagnetic and thermal fields under industrial operating conditions. The framework incorporates parameterized geometry generation and semi-automated, physics-tailored mesh construction and is implemented using the open-source tools GetDP and Gmsh. Validation against measurements from a commercial induction welding line for AISI 304 stainless steel tubes demonstrates good agreement with operating data. The validated model is subsequently applied to investigate the influence of impeder material by comparing a conventional FeNiZnV ferrite with the soft magnetic composite Ferrotron 559H for the induction welding of AISI 304 stainless steel tubes.

AI.tldr: A 3D multiphysics finite element framework for simulating high-frequency induction welding of tubes is presented, coupling a time-harmonic magnetic scalar potential formulation with a stabilized quasi-stationary advection-diffusion heat equation, implemented in GetDP and Gmsh, validated against a commercial AISI 304 line, and applied to compare impeder materials (FeNiZnV ferrite vs. Ferrotron 559H soft magnetic composite).
AI.motivation: Accurate prediction of electromagnetic and thermal fields in high-frequency induction welding of tubes under industrial operating conditions is needed, and there is interest in evaluating the influence of impeder material choice (conventional ferrite versus soft magnetic composite) on the process.
AI.method: A three-dimensional multiphysics finite element framework that couples a time-harmonic magnetic scalar potential formulation with a stabilized quasi-stationary advection-diffusion heat transport equation, incorporating parameterized geometry generation and semi-automated, physics-tailored mesh construction, implemented with the open-source tools GetDP and Gmsh.
AI.result: Validation against measurements from a commercial induction welding line for AISI 304 stainless steel tubes demonstrates good agreement with operating data. The model is then applied to compare a conventional FeNiZnV ferrite impeder with the soft magnetic composite Ferrotron 559H.
AI.conclusion: The validated framework enables accurate simulation of industrial high-frequency induction tube welding and provides a basis for assessing impeder material selection, comparing conventional FeNiZnV ferrite with Ferrotron 559H soft magnetic composite for AISI 304 tubes.

title: On the physical origins of switching diversity in Cu-embedded SiO$_x$ memristive devices
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, Supplementary Information included at the end of the same PDF
summary: Resistive switching devices with sub-stoichiometric SiO$_x$ and pancake-like Cu nanoparticles (Cu-PCs) exhibit distinct macroscopic current-voltage characteristics classified as capacitive or gradual (interface-type switching) and abrupt or resistive (filamentary-type switching), motivating an analysis of the microscopic processes underlying this diversity. It is proposed that the device defect landscape is largely shaped by two charged defect types, mobile oxygen vacancies and immobile Cu-related defects, whose distributions jointly govern interfacial and bulk transport. An effective one-dimensional cloud-in-a-cell simulation framework is employed to reproduce the phenomenological picture of both interface-type and filamentary-type switching by incorporating the dominant coupled ionic and electronic processes underlying these mechanisms. The model includes oxygen-vacancy drift-diffusion, Schottky-limited injection at the metal/oxide interfaces, and bulk trap-assisted transport via Poole-Frenkel conduction, with Cu-PCs near the top interface treated effectively. A simulation-based parametric study varying voltage stress, sweep rate, and oxide thickness is used to examine how these factors rebalance voltage partitioning and the spatiotemporal electric field distribution, thereby altering vacancy redistribution and the relative contributions of interface- and bulk-limited conduction. Using representative, physically motivated parameter sets informed by prior device-level studies, the simulations accurately reproduce the characteristic $I$-$V$ signatures of seven different experimentally observed switching responses. Overall, the findings help to link microscopic defect landscapes and transport processes to experimentally measured macroscopic responses within a single, self-consistent modeling framework.

AI.tldr: A 1D cloud-in-a-cell simulation framework, combining oxygen-vacancy drift-diffusion, Schottky injection, and Poole-Frenkel bulk transport with immobile Cu-related defects, reproduces both interface-type and filamentary-type switching in SiO$_x$/Cu-nanoparticle devices and links microscopic defect landscapes to macroscopic $I$-$V$ responses.
AI.motivation: Resistive switching devices based on sub-stoichiometric SiO$_x$ with pancake-like Cu nanoparticles show two distinct macroscopic $I$-$V$ behaviors—capacitive/gradual (interface-type) and abrupt/resistive (filamentary-type)—yet the microscopic processes causing this diversity remain unclear. A unified, self-consistent understanding of how defect distributions govern these different switching modes is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose that the defect landscape is dominated by two charged defect types: mobile oxygen vacancies and immobile Cu-related defects, whose distributions jointly control interfacial and bulk transport. They employ an effective 1D cloud-in-a-cell simulation framework incorporating coupled ionic and electronic processes: oxygen-vacancy drift-diffusion, Schottky-limited injection at metal/oxide interfaces, bulk trap-assisted Poole-Frenkel conduction, and effective treatment of Cu-PCs near the top interface. A parametric study varies voltage stress, sweep rate, and oxide thickness.
AI.result: The parametric study shows how voltage stress, sweep rate, and oxide thickness rebalance voltage partitioning and the spatiotemporal electric field distribution, altering vacancy redistribution and the relative contributions of interface- and bulk-limited conduction. With representative, physically motivated parameter sets informed by prior device-level studies, the simulations accurately reproduce the characteristic $I$-$V$ signatures of seven different experimentally observed switching responses.
AI.conclusion: The findings link microscopic defect landscapes and transport processes to experimentally measured macroscopic responses within a single, self-consistent modeling framework, offering a unified description of the diverse switching behaviors in SiO$_x$/Cu-PC devices.

title: Quantum interference between vortex- and impurity-bound states boosts thermoelectricity
summary: Thermoelectric effects in superconductors are generally suppressed by the approximate particle-hole symmetry of the quasiparticle spectrum, but can become pronounced near defects that host particle-hole asymmetric bound states. Here, we investigate how the local thermoelectric response is modified when multiple vortices or nonmagnetic impurities are brought into proximity. Using a lattice Bogolioubov-de Gennes approach combined with linear-response tunneling theory, we calculate the spatially resolved density of states and Seebeck coefficient in $s$- and $d$-wave superconductors. We find that the thermoelectric response can be strongly enhanced when spatially extended defect-induced states overlap. For vortices, this enhancement persists beyond the immediate core regions and originates from interference between vortex-bound states. For impurities, the thermoelectric response exhibits a comparable dependence on impurity separation in the $s$- and $d$-wave cases, although the associated spectral reconstruction is considerably more localized in the $s$-wave superconductor. Our results show that the spatial extent and interference of defect-induced quasiparticle states provide a means of controlling local thermoelectricity in inhomogeneous superconductors, with potential relevance for cryogenic thermoelectric sensing and energy conversion.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how the local thermoelectric response (Seebeck coefficient) of superconductors is enhanced when multiple vortices or nonmagnetic impurities are close enough for their defect-induced quasiparticle states to overlap and interfere. Using lattice Bogoliubov-de Gennes calculations with linear-response tunneling theory for s- and d-wave superconductors, it shows that overlapping defect states strongly boost thermoelectricity beyond the immediate core regions, offering a route to control local thermoelectricity in inhomogeneous superconductors.
AI.motivation: Thermoelectric effects in superconductors are generally suppressed by the approximate particle-hole symmetry of the quasiparticle spectrum, but they can become pronounced near defects hosting particle-hole asymmetric bound states. The motivation is to understand how the local thermoelectric response is modified when multiple vortices or nonmagnetic impurities are brought into proximity, i.e., whether overlapping defect-induced states can further enhance thermoelectricity.
AI.method: A lattice Bogoliubov-de Gennes approach is combined with linear-response tunneling theory to compute the spatially resolved density of states and Seebeck coefficient in s-wave and d-wave superconductors, examining configurations with multiple vortices and nonmagnetic impurities at varying separations.
AI.result: The thermoelectric response can be strongly enhanced when spatially extended defect-induced states overlap. For vortices, the enhancement persists beyond the immediate core regions and originates from interference between vortex-bound states. For impurities, the thermoelectric response shows a comparable dependence on impurity separation in both s- and d-wave cases, although the associated spectral reconstruction is considerably more localized in the s-wave superconductor.
AI.conclusion: The spatial extent and interference of defect-induced quasiparticle states provide a means of controlling local thermoelectricity in inhomogeneous superconductors, with potential relevance for cryogenic thermoelectric sensing and energy conversion.

title: Breaking Water at Graphene Defects
summary: Water dissociation at solid surfaces underpins processes ranging from corrosion and catalysis to electrochemistry and photovoltaics. Defects often serve as reactive sites for dissociation, yet how solvation influences water dissociation at such sites remains poorly understood. Here, we use state-of-the-art machine-learned interatomic potentials to explore water dissociation at defective graphene-water interfaces. We show that solvation qualitatively changes the reaction mechanism at a graphene single vacancy (SV), opening pathways that are absent for an isolated water molecule. Whereas the gas-phase process proceeds via a single concerted channel, the solvated SV splits water through two competing pathways: a basic route forming SV-H and OH-(aq), and an acidic route forming SV-OH and H3O+(aq). These lower-barrier pathways produce distinct chemisorbed intermediates that enhance graphene-water adsorption. Accordingly, even a simple carbon vacancy gives rise to unexpectedly rich interfacial chemistry, coupling surface chemistry to interfacial charge and wettability, with implications for carbon functionalization and nanofluidic transport.

AI.tldr: Machine-learned interatomic potentials reveal that solvation qualitatively alters water dissociation at a graphene single vacancy, enabling two competing low-barrier pathways (basic: SV-H + OH⁻(aq); acidic: SV-OH + H₃O⁺(aq)) absent in the gas phase, enriching interfacial chemistry and wettability.
AI.motivation: Water dissociation at solid surfaces is central to corrosion, catalysis, electrochemistry, and photovoltaics. Although defects act as reactive sites, how solvation modulates dissociation at such sites is poorly understood.
AI.method: State-of-the-art machine-learned interatomic potentials were used to simulate water dissociation at defective graphene-water interfaces, specifically at a graphene single vacancy (SV), comparing gas-phase and solvated mechanisms.
AI.result: In the gas phase, dissociation proceeds via a single concerted channel. Under solvation, the SV splits water through two competing pathways: a basic route forming SV-H and OH⁻(aq), and an acidic route forming SV-OH and H₃O⁺(aq). These lower-barrier pathways yield distinct chemisorbed intermediates that enhance graphene-water adsorption.
AI.conclusion: Even a simple carbon vacancy produces unexpectedly rich interfacial chemistry, coupling surface chemistry to interfacial charge and wettability, with implications for carbon functionalization and nanofluidic transport.

title: Dissipation-induced nonlocal phase-coherent transport in a topological superconductor
summary: Nonlocal phase-coherent transport via Majorana bound states, so-called teleportation, requires Coulomb blockade to suppress local Andreev reflection. We show that dissipation can replace the need for Coulomb blockade. We study a Kitaev chain coupled to a Markovian bath and identify a regime where the magnitude of nonlocal conductance contribution reach the local one. In this regime, the lowest-energy subspace is maximally mixed, reminiscent of a directly-grounded nontrivial topological superconductor. Phase coherence is confirmed by Aharonov-Bohm oscillations. Our results establish dissipation as a tool for controlling quantum teleportation in Majorana systems.

AI.tldr: Dissipation, instead of Coulomb blockade, can enable phase-coherent nonlocal transport (teleportation) via Majorana bound states in a Kitaev chain coupled to a Markovian bath.
AI.motivation: Nonlocal phase-coherent transport via Majorana bound states (teleportation) conventionally requires Coulomb blockade to suppress local Andreev reflection. This is a stringent experimental constraint, motivating a search for alternative mechanisms that achieve the same suppression.
AI.method: A Kitaev chain is coupled to a Markovian bath (introducing dissipation), and the transport regime is analyzed to identify conditions where the nonlocal conductance contribution becomes comparable in magnitude to the local one.
AI.result: A regime is found where the nonlocal conductance contribution reaches the magnitude of the local one. In this regime, the lowest-energy subspace is maximally mixed, resembling a directly-grounded nontrivial topological superconductor. Phase coherence is confirmed via Aharonov-Bohm oscillations.
AI.conclusion: Dissipation can replace Coulomb blockade as a requirement for teleportation, establishing dissipation as a tool for controlling quantum teleportation in Majorana systems.

title: Rare-History Transitions in Temporally Random Integrable Quantum Circuits
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures. Supplemental Material will be submitted separately. This is an initial draft, and comments are welcome
summary: We study current fluctuations in a temporally random integrable quantum circuit. Commutativity reduces every drive history exactly to its layer composition, turning annealed fluctuations into a competition between current gain and the large-deviation cost of rare compositions. For each fixed composition, homogeneous thermodynamic Bethe ansatz dressing supplemented by ballistic fluctuation theory yields the conditional current statistics. Their annealed large-deviation contraction predicts a first-order switch between two dominant history classes, terminating on a line of regular cusp endpoints. Finite-time analysis shows how the switch is rounded. Thus temporal randomness can act as an emergent order-parameter-like coordinate in trajectory space.

AI.tldr: Current fluctuations in a temporally random integrable quantum circuit are reduced, via commutativity, to a competition between current gain and the large-deviation cost of rare layer compositions, yielding conditional statistics from thermodynamic Bethe ansatz dressing and ballistic fluctuation theory, predicting a first-order switch between dominant history classes ending on a line of regular cusps.
AI.motivation: Temporal randomness in integrable quantum circuits is expected to strongly affect current fluctuations, but how annealed fluctuations arise from the interplay of drive history and rare composition costs is not well understood.
AI.method: Commutativity is used to reduce every drive history exactly to its layer composition. For each fixed composition, homogeneous thermodynamic Bethe ansatz dressing combined with ballistic fluctuation theory gives the conditional current statistics; these are then contracted via annealed large-deviation theory, with finite-time analysis of the rounding.
AI.result: The annealed large-deviation contraction predicts a first-order switch between two dominant history classes, terminating on a line of regular cusp endpoints; finite-time analysis shows how this switch is rounded.
AI.conclusion: Temporal randomness can act as an emergent order-parameter-like coordinate in trajectory space, controlling a first-order transition between dominant history classes.

title: Non-stick vacuum wall collisions with a laser-coolable molecule
summary: Molecular species that are suitable for direct laser cooling are typically considered lost or destroyed if they collide with an ambient temperature vacuum wall. Here, we study surface collisions with aluminum monofluoride (AlF), a laser-coolable molecule that survives this process with unusually high probability. We detect the outgoing AlF molecules from a single wall collision via Doppler-sensitive laser-induced fluorescence spectroscopy, using incoming supersonic (pulsed) and thermochemical (continuous) molecular beams. The angular, velocity and rovibrational level distributions of the outgoing molecules show near-complete thermalisation to the wall in a single collision event. We determine an upper limit to the surface residence time of about 5$~μ$s, and by monitoring the decay in density of pulses of molecules loaded into a small storage volume, we deduce the surface sticking probability for different materials. For a siloxane-coated metallic surface, the sticking probability of AlF is about 0.015, allowing us to accumulate molecules from the thermochemical source into an ambient temperature storage vessel at densities near $10^{8}~$cm$^{-3}$. This provides a route to compact, portable traps for neutral molecules.

AI.tldr: AlF molecules survive collisions with room-temperature walls with high probability (sticking probability ~0.015 on siloxane-coated metal), enabling accumulation of ~10^8 cm^-3 in an ambient-temperature storage vessel and a route to compact neutral-molecule traps.
AI.motivation: Directly laser-coolable molecular species are generally assumed to be lost or destroyed upon colliding with an ambient-temperature vacuum wall. This limits their use in compact, portable devices and motivates investigating whether any laser-coolable molecule can survive surface collisions.
AI.method: Surface collisions of aluminum monofluoride (AlF) with walls were studied using Doppler-sensitive laser-induced fluorescence spectroscopy of outgoing molecules, with both supersonic pulsed and thermochemical continuous molecular beams. Angular, velocity, and rovibrational level distributions were measured, the surface residence time was bounded, and sticking probabilities were deduced by monitoring density decay of molecule pulses in a small storage volume for different materials.
AI.result: Outgoing AlF shows near-complete thermalisation to the wall in a single collision (angular, velocity, rovibrational distributions). Upper limit on surface residence time ~5 μs. Sticking probability on siloxane-coated metallic surface ~0.015, enabling accumulation of molecules from a thermochemical source in an ambient-temperature storage vessel at densities near 10^8 cm^-3.
AI.conclusion: AlF is a laser-coolable molecule that survives ambient-temperature wall collisions with unusually high probability, allowing compact ambient-temperature storage and providing a route toward portable traps for neutral molecules.

title: Influence of magnetic fields on the performance of spin-orbit torque magnetic random-access memory
comment: English translated version of the original Chinese paper published in Acta Physica Sinica. 17 pages, 13 figures, 1 table
summary: Spin-orbit torque magnetic random-access memory (SOT-MRAM) offers high speed, ultrahigh endurance, and compatibility with advanced semiconductor processes, making it a promising candidate for next-generation nonvolatile memory. However, intrinsic bias fields in magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs), originating from reference-layer stray fields and interlayer coupling, cause asymmetric critical switching currents and increased energy consumption. Existing compensation approaches usually introduce additional magnetic layers into the MTJ stack, which increases fabrication complexity and limits wafer-scale integration. Here, we propose a bias-compensation strategy without modifying the MTJ stack by engineering local stray magnetic fields through magnetic filling materials in vertical interconnect access (VIA) channels during the back-end-of-line process. Micromagnetic simulations show that the proposed magnetic filling layer can provide the required auxiliary field for deterministic switching and significantly suppress write-current asymmetry. By optimizing the MTJ position relative to the magnetic filling structure, the write-current bias ratio is reduced from 21.6% in the conventional design to 1.3%. The approach is also applicable to in-plane magnetic anisotropy SOT-MTJs, reducing the bias ratio from 19.8% to -0.2%. Scaling analysis further demonstrates that the compensation effect remains effective when the device size is reduced to 20% of the original dimension (MTJ diameter approximately 10 nm), indicating its potential for high-density SOT-MRAM integration.

AI.tldr: This work proposes compensating the intrinsic bias field of SOT-MTJs by engineering local stray fields via magnetic filling materials in VIA channels during BEOL, avoiding any MTJ stack modification and reducing the write-current bias ratio to ~1%.
