AI.motivation: SOT-MRAM suffers from intrinsic bias fields in MTJs arising from reference-layer stray fields and interlayer coupling, which cause asymmetric critical switching currents and higher energy consumption. Existing compensation schemes add extra magnetic layers into the MTJ stack, increasing fabrication complexity and limiting wafer-scale integration, so a stack-free compensation method is needed.
AI.method: Instead of modifying the MTJ stack, local stray magnetic fields are engineered using magnetic filling materials placed in vertical interconnect access (VIA) channels during the back-end-of-line (BEOL) process. Micromagnetic simulations are used to evaluate the auxiliary field and switching behavior, and the MTJ position relative to the magnetic filling structure is optimized.
AI.result: The magnetic filling layer provides the auxiliary field required for deterministic switching and significantly suppresses write-current asymmetry. Optimizing MTJ placement reduces the write-current bias ratio from 21.6% (conventional) to 1.3%. For in-plane magnetic anisotropy SOT-MTJs, the bias ratio drops from 19.8% to -0.2%. Scaling analysis shows the compensation remains effective down to 20% of the original device size (MTJ diameter ~10 nm).
AI.conclusion: Bias-field compensation via magnetic VIA filling is an effective, stack-compatible route to symmetric SOT-MTJ switching, maintaining efficacy at aggressively scaled dimensions and showing strong potential for high-density SOT-MRAM integration.

title: A Unified Theory of Collective Magnon and Orbiton Excitations in Altermagnets
comment: 37 pages (19 pages main, 18 pages supplement), 5 figures (all in main), 1 table (in main)
summary: Altermagnetism has recently emerged as a distinct collinear magnetic phase exhibiting momentum-dependent spin-splitting despite vanishing net magnetization, as a consequence of inequivalent non-magnetic environments. Lately, it has been proposed that strong electronic correlations may yield spontaneous altermagnetism due to orbital ordering even for equivalent non-magnetic environments. While previous studies have largely focused on the electronic structure, a unified understanding of the collective excitations associated with these two different microscopic mechanisms stabilizing altermagnetism remains absent. Here, we develop an extended Kugel'-Khomskiĭ spin-orbital model on a decorated square lattice that simultaneously incorporates inequivalent non-magnetic environments and correlation-driven orbital ordering within a common theoretical framework. Employing a self-consistent mean-field spin-wave orbital-wave formalism, we demonstrate the emergence of mutually unhybridized but interdependent magnon and orbiton excitations exhibiting characteristic chiral-splitting. We show that the splitting originates from two distinct microscopic contributions: a lattice-dependent term arising from inequivalent non-magnetic environments and an orbital-order-induced exchange-anisotropy term that survives even for equivalent non-magnetic environments. The proposed framework therefore unifies the collective excitations associated with both types of altermagnetism. We further investigate the finite-temperature evolution of the coupled spin-orbital system, revealing the breakdown of spin-wave and orbital-wave approximations through spurious 1st-order transitions, while complementary classical Monte Carlo simulations recover the expected continuous 2nd-order behaviour. Our work establishes a unified microscopic framework for understanding collective magnon and orbiton excitations in altermagnets.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a unified Kugel'-Khomskiĭ spin-orbital model on a decorated square lattice to describe collective magnon and orbiton excitations in altermagnets stabilized by two distinct mechanisms: inequivalent non-magnetic environments and correlation-driven orbital ordering.
AI.motivation: Altermagnetism is a distinct collinear magnetic phase with momentum-dependent spin-splitting but zero net magnetization. Recent proposals suggest spontaneous altermagnetism can arise from strong electronic correlations via orbital ordering even for equivalent non-magnetic environments. However, a unified understanding of the collective excitations associated with these two different microscopic mechanisms stabilizing altermagnetism is absent.
AI.method: The authors develop an extended Kugel'-Khomskiĭ spin-orbital model on a decorated square lattice that simultaneously incorporates inequivalent non-magnetic environments and correlation-driven orbital ordering. They employ a self-consistent mean-field spin-wave and orbital-wave formalism to obtain collective excitations, and complementary classical Monte Carlo simulations to examine finite-temperature behavior.
AI.result: The model yields mutually unhybridized but interdependent magnon and orbiton excitations with characteristic chiral-splitting. The splitting arises from two microscopic contributions: a lattice-dependent term from inequivalent non-magnetic environments and an orbital-order-induced exchange-anisotropy term that survives even for equivalent environments. Finite-temperature analysis shows the spin-wave and orbital-wave approximations break down through spurious first-order transitions, while classical Monte Carlo recovers the expected continuous second-order behavior.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a unified microscopic framework for understanding collective magnon and orbiton excitations in altermagnets, bridging the two mechanisms (inequivalent non-magnetic environments and correlation-driven orbital ordering) within a single theoretical description.

title: Stress-Testing Dynamical and Generative Downscaling Using Subseasonal Extreme Precipitation Forecasts
comment: 36 pages, 12 figures, 6 tables, submitted to JAMES
summary: Coarse spatial resolution limits the ability of subseasonal prediction models to resolve extreme precipitation. Downscaling with either dynamical or deep generative models can overcome this issue, but the comparative performance of these models for extremes across different atmospheric regimes remains poorly understood. In this work, we evaluate the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model against a diffusion-based generative model by downscaling two physically distinct, extreme precipitation events up to lead times of 3 weeks. For a fair comparison with WRF, which can downscale boundary conditions from different driving models without model-specific training, the diffusion model is trained in an unpaired fashion. Both approaches improve upon the raw European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts forecasts, in comparison to fused rain gauge-radar observations in Switzerland (CombiPrecip), but exhibit regime-dependent strengths. WRF achieves the highest probabilistic skill for a multicell, non-stationary event. Conversely, the diffusion model is more consistent across different performance metrics for the two events, outperforming WRF in a more stationary supercell event. These results demonstrate that explicit dynamical modeling can add value for specific precipitation events for subseasonal lead times, and that generative downscaling adds value more broadly in different situations.

AI.tldr: WRF and a diffusion-based generative model both downscale subseasonal extreme precipitation better than raw ECMWF forecasts, but with regime-dependent skill: WRF excels for a non-stationary multicell event, while the diffusion model is more consistent and wins for a stationary supercell event.
AI.motivation: Coarse spatial resolution limits subseasonal models' ability to resolve extreme precipitation. While dynamical and deep generative downscaling can address this, their comparative performance across different atmospheric regimes is poorly understood.
AI.method: Downscale two physically distinct extreme precipitation events up to 3-week lead times using (1) the WRF dynamical model and (2) a diffusion-based generative model trained in an unpaired fashion to allow fair comparison with WRF's training-free boundary-condition downscaling. Evaluate against fused rain gauge-radar observations (CombiPrecip) in Switzerland.
AI.result: Both methods improve on raw ECMWF forecasts but show regime-dependent strengths. WRF achieves the highest probabilistic skill for a multicell, non-stationary event; the diffusion model is more consistent across metrics and outperforms WRF for a more stationary supercell event.
AI.conclusion: Explicit dynamical modeling (WRF) adds value for specific precipitation events at subseasonal lead times, whereas generative downscaling adds value more broadly across different situations.

title: Hyperspin Altermagnets
summary: The behavior of spin quantum in k-space is key to identifying altermagnets (AMs) as the third kind of fundamental collinear magnetism. In contrast, non-collinear magnets,though abundant in nature,lack well-defined spin quantum numbers, and the resulting spin textures are often highly complex, which limits their potential for next-generation spintronic applications. Here we propose hyperspin, which lives in a higher-dimensional space, to address these drawbacks. Through analyzing the commutation relations between spin and Hamiltonian for a class of non-collinear magnets, we reveal it is a hyperspin, rather than the usual spin, that commutes with Hamiltonian. Unexpectedly, these non-collinear magnets should also show collinear spin-split bands in k-space like collinear AMs. We therefore classify such non-collinear magnets as hyperspin altermagnets (HAMs), as opposed to the usual collinear AMs. Our theory elucidates the fundamental physics of AMs and HAMs and provides a framework for exploring the wide range of non-collinear magnets that may possess other kinds of conserved quantities.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "hyperspin," a conserved quantity living in a higher-dimensional space, to describe a class of non-collinear magnets that exhibit collinear spin-split bands in k-space, analogous to collinear altermagnets.
AI.motivation: Altermagnets (AMs) are identified as the third kind of fundamental collinear magnetism via spin quantum behavior in k-space, but non-collinear magnets—abundant in nature—lack well-defined spin quantum numbers, yielding complex spin textures that limit their spintronic potential.
AI.method: The authors analyze the commutation relations between spin and the Hamiltonian for a class of non-collinear magnets, revealing that a hyperspin—not the usual spin—commutes with the Hamiltonian.
AI.result: It is found that these non-collinear magnets exhibit collinear spin-split bands in k-space, similar to collinear AMs, leading to their classification as hyperspin altermagnets (HAMs).
AI.conclusion: The theory clarifies the fundamental physics of AMs and HAMs and offers a framework for exploring non-collinear magnets that may host other kinds of conserved quantities.

title: Dissipative quantum mechanics of Andreev bound states
summary: We propose a microscopic scheme that allows to describe ac Josephson effect in superconducting junctions in terms of dissipative quantum dynamics of subgap Andreev bound states. This approach is particularly useful for highly transparent junctions at subgap bias voltages in which case a non-trivial combination of Landau-Zener tunneling between Andreev levels and their instability due to quasiparticle escape into continuum may play an important role. In the low bias regime, we evaluate the non-equilibrium current-phase relation of superconducting junctions at arbitrary transmissions and identify a sub-Ohmic phase-dependent dissipative contribution to the current controlled by quasiparticle dynamics near the superconducting gap edge.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a microscopic scheme describing the ac Josephson effect via dissipative quantum dynamics of subgap Andreev bound states, and derives a non-equilibrium current-phase relation with a sub-Ohmic dissipative contribution.
AI.motivation: Highly transparent superconducting junctions at subgap bias voltages exhibit nontrivial interplay between Landau-Zener tunneling between Andreev levels and their instability due to quasiparticle escape into the continuum, motivating a description beyond standard approaches.
AI.method: A microscopic scheme based on dissipative quantum dynamics of subgap Andreev bound states is developed, treating Landau-Zener tunneling and quasiparticle escape into the continuum.
AI.result: In the low bias regime, the non-equilibrium current-phase relation of superconducting junctions at arbitrary transmissions is evaluated, and a sub-Ohmic phase-dependent dissipative contribution to the current is identified, controlled by quasiparticle dynamics near the gap edge.
AI.conclusion: The ac Josephson effect can be described microscopically through dissipative dynamics of Andreev bound states, yielding a characteristic sub-Ohmic dissipative current contribution governed by quasiparticle processes near the superconducting gap edge.

title: Controlling topology in flux-mismatched Hofstadter bilayers
summary: Stacked two-dimensional materials provide a promising platform for electrically controlling topological electronic states. However, tunneling between layers hybridizes their bands and removes the crossings needed to change topology. We show that this does not always have to be the case. Band crossings and associated Weyl points are topologically enforced in Hofstadter bilayers whose layers experience different magnetic fluxes. When resonant magnetic Bloch multiplets carry unequal Chern numbers, their projected tunneling is topologically obstructed and must vanish at isolated momenta. Sweeping the layer bias through these zeros creates synthetic Weyl monopoles in momentum-bias space that transfer the Chern mismatch. We demonstrate two consequences: a direct transition between insulating Chern phases and a reentrant compensated metal in which Lifshitz transitions bound the metallic window while internal Weyl events reconstruct the band topology. Consequently, the fixed-filling Hall response remains continuous and nonquantized even as integer Chern number is transferred between bands. Berry-flux, TKNN, and interface calculations independently verify the mechanism and its multichannel chiral signature. We outline realizations in Moire and anomalous-Hall heterostructures, establishing flux mismatch as an experimentally accessible route to electrically programmable Chern phases and chiral transport.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that band crossings and Weyl points are topologically enforced in Hofstadter bilayers with flux mismatch, enabling electrical control of Chern phases and chiral transport.
AI.motivation: Stacked two-dimensional materials are promising for electrically controlling topological electronic states, but interlayer tunneling hybridizes bands and removes the crossings needed to change topology. This work asks whether such crossings can instead be topologically protected.
AI.method: The authors study Hofstadter bilayers whose layers experience different magnetic fluxes. They analyze resonant magnetic Bloch multiplets carrying unequal Chern numbers, showing projected tunneling is topologically obstructed and must vanish at isolated momenta. Sweeping the layer bias through these zeros creates synthetic Weyl monopoles in momentum-bias space. Berry-flux, TKNN, and interface calculations are used to verify the mechanism.
AI.result: The mechanism produces two consequences: a direct transition between insulating Chern phases, and a reentrant compensated metal in which Lifshitz transitions bound the metallic window while internal Weyl events reconstruct band topology. The fixed-filling Hall response remains continuous and nonquantized even as integer Chern number is transferred between bands, with a multichannel chiral signature.
AI.conclusion: Flux mismatch establishes an experimentally accessible route to electrically programmable Chern phases and chiral transport, with outlined realizations in Moire and anomalous-Hall heterostructures.

title: Work as a function of protocol duration for the efficient erasure of an underdamped memory: isothermal to adiabatic transition
summary: We use evolutionary reinforcement learning to determine efficient time-dependent erasure protocols for an underdamped cantilever moving in a double-well potential, an experimental realization of a 1-bit memory. We investigate how the mean work $\langle W \rangle $ needed to erase a bit scales as a function of the protocol duration $τ$. We find two regimes, depending on how $τ$ compares to the relaxation time of the system $t_r$. For $τ\gg t_r$, the quasistatic isothermal regime, we recover Landauer's bound plus an overhead that scales as $1/τ$, similar to the overdamped case. By contrast, for $τ<t_r$ erasure becomes adiabatic and $\langle W \rangle$ grows more slowly than in the isothermal case. This growth is bounded from below as $1/τ$, which we derive using a gedanken optimal protocol. Finally, comparison with overdamped erasure shows that learned protocols can outperform protocols that are optimal subject to equilibrium boundary conditions.

AI.tldr: Evolutionary reinforcement learning is used to find efficient time-dependent erasure protocols for an underdamped cantilever in a double-well potential (a 1-bit memory), revealing two work-scaling regimes separated by the relaxation time and showing learned protocols can beat equilibrium-boundary-optimal ones.
AI.motivation: To understand how the mean work required to erase a bit scales with protocol duration in an underdamped (rather than the more commonly studied overdamped) system, an experimental 1-bit memory realized by a cantilever in a double-well potential.
AI.method: Evolutionary reinforcement learning is applied to design efficient time-dependent erasure protocols for an underdamped cantilever moving in a double-well potential. The scaling of mean work ⟨W⟩ with protocol duration τ is analyzed relative to the system relaxation time t_r, supported by a gedanken optimal protocol for a lower bound and by comparison against overdamped erasure protocols optimal under equilibrium boundary conditions.
AI.result: Two regimes emerge. For τ ≫ t_r (quasistatic isothermal regime), Landauer's bound is recovered plus an overhead scaling as 1/τ, as in the overdamped case. For τ < t_r, erasure becomes adiabatic and ⟨W⟩ grows more slowly than isothermally, with a lower-bounded growth of 1/τ derived from a gedanken optimal protocol. Learned protocols can outperform those optimal subject to equilibrium boundary conditions.
AI.conclusion: The work cost of erasing an underdamped 1-bit memory exhibits distinct isothermal (τ ≫ t_r) and adiabatic (τ < t_r) scaling regimes, with adiabatic erasure growing more slowly and bounded below by 1/τ. Reinforcement-learned protocols can surpass equilibrium-boundary-optimal protocols, underscoring the value of learning-based protocol design for finite-time information erasure.

title: Kinetic modeling of molecular beam formation in a cryogenic buffer-gas cell
summary: Cryogenic buffer-gas cells are widely used to produce cold molecular beams, but the microscopic dynamics governing beam formation remain challenging to model. Here we present fully kinetic simulations of a cryogenic buffer-gas cell using the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo method implemented in the PICLas framework, treating the buffer gas and ablated molecules within a single unified model. We capture characteristic features of cryogenic buffer-gas sources, including plume cooling, directed transport toward the aperture, and the formation of a slow molecular beam, while also resolving energy transfer from the hot ablation plume to the helium buffer gas that is inaccessible to existing approaches relying on the background-gas approximation. Our results demonstrate that fully kinetic simulations can provide detailed insights into buffer-gas cell dynamics and open a route toward a systematic optimization of such sources.

AI.tldr: Fully kinetic DSMC simulations in PICLas model a cryogenic buffer-gas cell with buffer gas and ablated molecules in one unified framework, reproducing plume cooling, directed transport, and slow beam formation while resolving plume-to-helium energy transfer inaccessible to background-gas approximations.
AI.motivation: Cryogenic buffer-gas cells are widely used to produce cold molecular beams, but the microscopic dynamics governing beam formation remain challenging to model; existing approaches rely on a background-gas approximation that cannot capture energy transfer from the hot ablation plume to the helium buffer gas.
AI.method: Fully kinetic simulations of a cryogenic buffer-gas cell using the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method implemented in the PICLas framework, treating the buffer gas and ablated molecules within a single unified model.
AI.result: The simulations capture characteristic features of cryogenic buffer-gas sources, including plume cooling, directed transport toward the aperture, and the formation of a slow molecular beam, while also resolving energy transfer from the hot ablation plume to the helium buffer gas.
AI.conclusion: Fully kinetic simulations provide detailed insights into buffer-gas cell dynamics and open a route toward systematic optimization of such sources.

title: Bottom-up Synthesis of Metastable 2D Hexagonal Copper(I) Iodide on Monolayer and within Bilayer Graphene
comment: 26 pages, 6 figures, Includes Supporting Information with 5 figures and 7 tables
summary: Copper(I) iodide (CuI) is a wide-bandgap semiconductor crystallizing in the 3D $γ$-phase under ambient conditions; its layered van der Waals bulk phase $β$-CuI is stable only between 643 and 673 K. The two-dimensional (2D) h-CuI form has been obtained via liquid-phase exfoliation of mechanochemically prepared precursors and via encapsulation between graphene sheets, whereas bottom-up growth of 2D h-CuI on open surfaces has not yet been demonstrated. Here, we report a vapor-phase synthesis of h-CuI directly on low-defect, large-area monolayer and within bilayer reduced oxo-graphene (r-oxo-G) at low temperatures. Using a copper TEM grid as the solid-state precursor for copper, HI-vapor exposure at 40 $°$C initiates nucleation, while annealing at 180 $°$C promotes the growth of extended h-CuI domains. Aberration-corrected HRTEM resolves the atomic structure, local twist angles, and lattice anisotropy of the CuI/r-oxo-G nanohybrid, while STEM-EDX yields a Cu:I ratio consistent with 1:1. First-principles calculations show that van der Waals adhesion to graphene stabilizes the supported hexagonal layer. Under the presented low-temperature precursor conditions, pathways for nucleation of the $γ$-phase are not available, allowing the hexagonal phase to form selectively at the graphene interface. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations show that the heterostructure retains its hexagonal lattice order at 600 K, including on an open monolayer graphene support. The lateral extent of the growth is limited mainly by remaining interfacial adsorbates. These results establish a route to metastable 2D h-CuI on a chemically inert graphene template, which may be useful for wide-bandgap electronic and optoelectronic devices.

AI.tldr: A low-temperature vapor-phase route grows metastable 2D hexagonal CuI directly on monolayer/bilayer reduced oxo-graphene, using a Cu TEM grid and HI vapor, yielding a stable wide-bandgap CuI/graphene nanohybrid.
AI.motivation: CuI normally crystallizes in the 3D gamma-phase at ambient conditions; its layered van der Waals beta-phase is stable only at 643-673 K. While 2D h-CuI has been made by liquid-phase exfoliation or graphene encapsulation, bottom-up growth on open surfaces has not been demonstrated. The authors aim to grow 2D h-CuI directly on a chemically inert graphene template.
AI.method: Vapor-phase synthesis on low-defect, large-area monolayer and within bilayer reduced oxo-graphene (r-oxo-G). A copper TEM grid serves as solid-state Cu precursor; HI-vapor exposure at 40 C initiates nucleation, and annealing at 180 C promotes growth of extended h-CuI domains. Characterization by aberration-corrected HRTEM (atomic structure, twist angles, lattice anisotropy), STEM-EDX (Cu:I ~1:1), first-principles calculations (van der Waals adhesion stabilizes the hexagonal layer), and ab initio molecular dynamics (thermal stability).
AI.result: h-CuI grows selectively on r-oxo-G at low temperature; HRTEM resolves atomic structure, local twist angles, and lattice anisotropy of the CuI/r-oxo-G nanohybrid; STEM-EDX gives a Cu:I ratio consistent with 1:1. First-principles calculations show van der Waals adhesion to graphene stabilizes the supported hexagonal layer. Low-temperature precursor conditions suppress gamma-phase nucleation pathways, enabling selective hexagonal-phase formation at the graphene interface. AIMD shows the heterostructure retains hexagonal lattice order at 600 K, including on open monolayer graphene. Lateral growth extent is limited mainly by remaining interfacial adsorbates.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a route to metastable 2D h-CuI on a chemically inert graphene template, potentially useful for wide-bandgap electronic and optoelectronic devices.

title: Competing Interlayer Loop Currents and Superconductivity in the Bilayer $t$-$J_\perp$-$V$ Model
summary: The recent discovery of high-$T_c$ superconductivity in pressurized and thin-film bilayer nickelates, featuring a strong interlayer exchange coupling, and their potential similarities with cuprate superconductors, has made this a very active topic in condensed matter physics. In the present paper we study the strongly correlated one-orbital ($d_{x^2-y^2}$) bilayer $t$-$J_\perp$-$V$ model for nickelates, where $V$ denotes the Coulomb interactions, using a controlled large-$N$ expansion at and beyond the mean-field level. Focusing on the out-of-plane spin exchange interaction ($J_\perp$), we find that it triggers both out-of-plane $s$-wave superconductivity and an out-of-plane bond-order phase ($z$-BOP) instability. The $z$-BOP gives rise to a complex $z$-axis hopping dominated by its imaginary component, which drives out-of-plane currents and induces in-plane ones, spontaneously forming on the vertical plaquettes a loop-current state that breaks time-reversal symmetry. Competition between this loop-current phase and superconductivity yields a dome-shaped superconducting region, with optimal superconductivity occurring near the $z$-BOP quantum critical point. The resulting phase diagram features a pure loop-current region, a low-doping coexistence phase, a pure superconducting state at higher doping, and a correlated metallic state.

AI.tldr: Using a controlled large-N expansion of a one-orbital bilayer t-J_perp-V model for nickelates, the paper shows that interlayer exchange J_perp drives both out-of-plane s-wave superconductivity and a time-reversal-symmetry-breaking z-axis bond-order phase (loop-current state), whose competition produces a dome-shaped superconducting region peaked near the z-BOP quantum critical point.
AI.motivation: The discovery of high-Tc superconductivity in pressurized and thin-film bilayer nickelates, with strong interlayer exchange coupling and possible cuprate-like behavior, has made understanding the pairing mechanism and the interplay between superconductivity and other orders a central and active problem in condensed matter physics.
AI.method: The authors study the strongly correlated one-orbital (d_x2-y2) bilayer t-J_perp-V model, with V the Coulomb interaction, using a controlled large-N expansion at and beyond the mean-field level, focusing on the role of the out-of-plane spin exchange J_perp.
AI.result: J_perp triggers both out-of-plane s-wave superconductivity and an out-of-plane bond-order phase (z-BOP) instability. The z-BOP generates a complex z-axis hopping dominated by its imaginary part, driving out-of-plane currents that induce in-plane ones and spontaneously forming a loop-current state on vertical plaquettes that breaks time-reversal symmetry. Competition between the loop-current phase and superconductivity yields a dome-shaped superconducting region with optimal superconductivity near the z-BOP quantum critical point.
AI.conclusion: The resulting phase diagram contains a pure loop-current region, a low-doping coexistence phase of loop current and superconductivity, a pure superconducting state at higher doping, and a correlated metallic state.

title: Interface-Controlled Phase Stability in Polymorphic HfO$_2$ Revealed by Machine-Learning Atomistic Simulations
summary: HfO$_2$ exhibits rich polymorphism, and competition among different phases underpins many of its functional properties. Yet bulk free-energy relations alone cannot explain phase selection at mixed-phase boundaries, where interface orientation and structural continuity constrain collective rearrangements. Here, using machine-learning atomistic simulations and a Hf-centered local phase classification scheme, we show that crystallographic interface matching redirects phase competition and accessible transformation pathways. The M(100)/T(100) interface remains pinned as an M/T mixture throughout 3 ns simulations from 300 to 1800 K. M/PO, M/AO, and PO/AO interfaces retain two-phase coexistence up to 900 K, whereas all T/PO interfaces become PO-dominant. At 1800 K, all non-M interfaces become T-dominant, while M-containing interfaces retain a monoclinic majority. Nudged elastic band calculations reveal lower-barrier routes through interface states. For M(100)$\rightarrow$T(100), the interface-mediated route in a long cell ($\sim$12 nm) yields a barrier of 136.03 meV/f.u., 29.2 % lower than the direct route in a short cell ($\sim$3 nm). This difference is associated with sequential phase-front motion absent from the short cell. These results identify phase boundaries as active participants in phase stability and transformation and establish interface orientation and crystallographic matching as variables for stabilizing metastable polymorphs and directing phase conversion in HfO$_2$.

AI.tldr: Machine-learning atomistic simulations and nudged elastic band calculations reveal that crystallographic interface matching in HfO2 redirects phase competition, pins M/T mixtures, and lowers transformation barriers by up to 29.2% via interface-mediated pathways.
AI.motivation: Bulk free-energy relations alone cannot explain phase selection at mixed-phase boundaries in HfO2, where interface orientation and structural continuity constrain collective atomic rearrangements. Understanding how interfaces govern phase stability and transformation pathways is therefore necessary.
AI.method: Machine-learning atomistic simulations combined with a Hf-centered local phase classification scheme were used to track phase evolution at various interfaces (M/T, M/PO, M/AO, PO/AO, T/PO) from 300 to 1800 K over 3 ns. Nudged elastic band calculations compared interface-mediated and direct transformation routes in long (~12 nm) versus short (~3 nm) simulation cells.
AI.result: The M(100)/T(100) interface remained pinned as an M/T mixture across all temperatures. M/PO, M/AO, and PO/AO interfaces retained two-phase coexistence up to 900 K, while T/PO interfaces became PO-dominant. At 1800 K, all non-M interfaces became T-dominant, whereas M-containing interfaces retained a monoclinic majority. For M(100)→T(100), the interface-mediated route in the long cell had a barrier of 136.03 meV/f.u., 29.2% lower than the direct route in the short cell.
AI.conclusion: Phase boundaries act as active participants in phase stability and transformation, not passive boundaries. Interface orientation and crystallographic matching serve as controllable variables for stabilizing metastable polymorphs and directing phase conversion in HfO2.

title: Measuring chiral phonons
summary: Chiral phonons are quantized vibrations where the atomic motion in a solid breaks improper rotation symmetries. In many cases, chiral phonons possess angular momenta and are therefore selective to circularly polarized light. Both fundamental and applied research efforts on chiral phonons have been gaining increasing attention owing to their importance in a variety of fields including spintronics, spin-selective chemical reactions, thermal transport, quantum information processing and biosensing, where the bi-directional spin-lattice coupling enabled by chiral phonons can be harnessed in new ways, and potentially lead to new functionalities. Thus far, the studies of chiral phonons across diverse materials platforms have evolved largely independently within these fields, but the experimental techniques are often interrelated. In this perspective, we present a detailed description, as well as advantages and disadvantages of the current approaches for experimentally measuring chiral phonons in chiral and achiral materials. We conclude with a discussion of new methods for measuring chiral phonons. Ultimately, this work seeks to offer an experimental guide for systematically investigating the properties of chiral phonons in various materials systems and applications.

AI.tldr: This perspective reviews and compares experimental techniques for measuring chiral phonons in chiral and achiral materials, and proposes new measurement approaches.
AI.motivation: Chiral phonons—quantized vibrations whose atomic motion breaks improper rotation symmetries—carry angular momentum and couple selectively to circularly polarized light, making them relevant to spintronics, spin-selective chemistry, thermal transport, quantum information, and biosensing. Research across materials platforms has advanced largely in isolation, though the experimental methods are interrelated, so a unified experimental guide is needed.
AI.method: The authors provide a perspective-style critical survey of current experimental approaches for measuring chiral phonons in both chiral and achiral materials, detailing each technique's principles, advantages, and disadvantages, and then discuss emerging/new measurement methods.
AI.result: The paper catalogs and compares existing experimental techniques for chiral phonon detection, identifying their relative strengths and limitations, and highlights newly emerging methods for probing chiral phonons.
AI.conclusion: The work serves as an experimental guide for systematically investigating chiral phonon properties across diverse material systems and applications, aiming to bridge otherwise disconnected research efforts.

title: Out-of-equilibrium relaxation dynamics of the superconducting order parameter in CsV$_3$Sb$_5$
summary: The application of a time-varying strain field drives a superconducting order parameter out of equilibrium. How the order parameter relaxes back to equilibrium depends both on the structure of the superconducting gap and on the nature of quasiparticle scattering. We report the discovery of an ultrasonic attenuation peak inside the superconducting state of the kagome superconductor CsV$_3$Sb$_5$. This peak is the natural consequence of the order parameter relaxation time matching the ultrasonic drive frequency near $T_{\rm c}$. From the measured frequency dependence of the peak, we extract a microscopic scattering time of $τ_N = 25$ ps. This timescale is two orders of magnitude longer than the elastic scattering time as determined by resistivity measurements, but is comparable to the inelastic scattering time determined by thermal transport. Within the conventional framework of order-parameter relaxation, this implies that elastic scattering is ineffective at relaxing the superconducting condensate, consistent with a sign-preserving $s$-wave state obeying Anderson's theorem.

AI.tldr: Ultrasonic attenuation shows a peak inside the superconducting state of CsV₃Sb₅ due to order-parameter relaxation matching the drive frequency near T_c; the extracted scattering time τ_N = 25 ps implies elastic scattering is ineffective at relaxing the condensate, consistent with a sign-preserving s-wave state.
AI.motivation: Order-parameter relaxation dynamics depend on both the structure of the superconducting gap and the nature of quasiparticle scattering, so probing how the order parameter returns to equilibrium can reveal the gap symmetry and scattering mechanisms of the kagome superconductor CsV₃Sb₅.
AI.method: An ultrasonic attenuation experiment applying a time-varying strain field to drive the order parameter out of equilibrium. The measured frequency dependence of an attenuation peak arising when the order-parameter relaxation time matches the ultrasonic drive frequency near T_c is used to extract a microscopic scattering time.
AI.result: An ultrasonic attenuation peak is observed inside the superconducting state, yielding an extracted microscopic scattering time τ_N = 25 ps. This is two orders of magnitude longer than the elastic scattering time from resistivity but comparable to the inelastic scattering time from thermal transport.
AI.conclusion: Within the conventional order-parameter relaxation framework, elastic scattering is ineffective at relaxing the superconducting condensate in CsV₃Sb₅, consistent with a sign-preserving s-wave state obeying Anderson's theorem.

title: Emergence of spin-orbit coupling among spin, atomic orbital, and Bloch dynamics in Janus double-transition-metal MXenes
summary: We found a spin-orbit coupling to cause a simultaneous correlation among three degrees of freedom, the electronic spin, orbital, and Bloch dynamics in an investigation into the electronic structure of Janus double-transition-metal MXenes, Mo$_2$HfC$_2$OS and W$_2$HfC$_2$OS. In this paper, it is also revealed that the spin-orbit coupling causes a staggered spin configuration with a trigonal pattern around the $Γ$ point near the insulating gap. We developed a reduced Hamiltonian describing the electronic states and show that the spin-orbit coupling cannot be equated with conventional forms for a single electron in solids, LS, Rashba, and Dresselhaus couplings, even in the approximation under the low-energy and small wave number condition. Because of the intrinsic shape of the conduction band, a trigonally alternating spin-momentum locking emerges with the spin axis perpendicular to the layer plane. The theoretical analysis shows that these Janus materials can provide a platform for exploring the spin-related phenomena due to the trigonal spin-momentum locking other than Rashba and Dresselhaus types.

AI.tldr: Spin-orbit coupling in Janus MXenes Mo2HfC2OS and W2HfC2OS entangles electronic spin, orbital, and Bloch dynamics, producing a staggered trigonal spin texture near the Γ point that cannot be described by conventional LS, Rashba, or Dresselhaus couplings.
AI.motivation: Conventional single-electron spin-orbit coupling forms (LS, Rashba, Dresselhaus) may not capture the full physics of complex solids; the authors aim to identify and characterize a distinct spin-orbit-driven correlation among spin, orbital, and Bloch degrees of freedom in Janus double-transition-metal MXenes.
AI.method: Electronic structure investigation of Janus double-transition-metal MXenes Mo2HfC2OS and W2HfC2OS, combined with a reduced low-energy, small-wave-number Hamiltonian describing the electronic states near the Γ point.
AI.result: Spin-orbit coupling induces a simultaneous correlation of electronic spin, orbital, and Bloch dynamics and a staggered spin configuration with a trigonal pattern around the Γ point near the insulating gap. Due to the intrinsic conduction-band shape, a trigonally alternating spin-momentum locking emerges with the spin axis perpendicular to the layer plane.
AI.conclusion: The spin-orbit coupling in these Janus MXenes cannot be equated with conventional LS, Rashba, or Dresselhaus forms even in the low-energy, small-wave-number approximation. These materials provide a platform for exploring spin-related phenomena based on trigonal spin-momentum locking distinct from Rashba and Dresselhaus types.

title: Certified reduced-basis emulation of conformal field theories on the fuzzy sphere
summary: Fuzzy-sphere regularization gives numerical access to three-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs), but locating one requires testing for criticality across the parameter space of microscopic couplings. We reduce the search cost by about two orders of magnitude, combining an exact diagonalization based on states having definite total angular momentum with a certified reduced-basis emulator that reconstructs energies, observables and their derivatives continuously across the couplings from a handful of exact solutions per system size. The combination reproduces the published ground-state-energy analysis of the fuzzy-sphere Ising model and the published conformal data of a three-flavor fuzzy-sphere realization of the O(2) Wilson--Fisher CFT, including quantities defined by parameter derivatives. Applied to the O(2) model with no CFT input, the ground-state-energy criterion locates the critical coupling to within half a percent of a density matrix renormalization group value obtained on systems more than twice the size, and maps the critical line of the model across the coupling plane. Ground-state criteria locate the critical line robustly, but the point they select along it is weakly determined, and the computed dimensions come closest to the bootstrap elsewhere along the line.

AI.tldr: Combining angular-momentum-resolved exact diagonalization with a certified reduced-basis emulator cuts the cost of locating 3D CFTs on the fuzzy sphere by ~two orders of magnitude, reproducing published Ising and O(2) results and mapping the O(2) critical line.
AI.motivation: Fuzzy-sphere regularization provides numerical access to 3D CFTs, but finding a critical point requires scanning the microscopic coupling parameter space for criticality, which is computationally expensive.
AI.method: Exact diagonalization restricted to states of definite total angular momentum, combined with a certified reduced-basis emulator that reconstructs energies, observables, and their coupling derivatives continuously from a few exact solutions per system size.
AI.result: Reproduces the published ground-state-energy analysis of the fuzzy-sphere Ising model and the published conformal data of a three-flavor fuzzy-sphere O(2) Wilson-Fisher CFT, including parameter-derivative quantities. With no CFT input, the ground-state-energy criterion locates the O(2) critical coupling within 0.5% of a DMRG value from systems over twice as large, and maps the critical line across the coupling plane.
AI.conclusion: Ground-state criteria robustly locate the critical line, but the selected point along it is weakly determined; computed dimensions approach the bootstrap result best elsewhere along the line.

title: Impact of Raman lasers beam profile inhomogeneities on a spaceborne quantum accelerometer
summary: We report on the study of the impact of laser beam profile inhomogeneities on the acceleration measurements of a quantum accelerometer in space. This sensor uses a low ballistic expansion source based on delta-kick collimated Bose-Einstein condensates, and an interferometer configuration based on a sequence of Raman double diffraction beamsplitters, best suited to the microgravity environment. We characterize both phase and intensity fluctuations in terms of power spectral densities and calculate their impact on the interferometer phase, averaging over all trajectories of the atoms, via numerical simulations based on randomly drawn laser profiles as well as via analytical treatments. We show that high quality optics, such as those realized for gravitational wave detectors, combined with large initial size atomic sources, will allow to reduce interferometer phase bias and fluctuations to the order of 1 mrad corresponding to accelerations in the low 10 -12 m.s -2 range.

AI.tldr: This work evaluates how laser beam profile inhomogeneities affect interferometer phase and acceleration measurements in a space-based quantum accelerometer using delta-kick collimated BECs and Raman double-diffraction beamsplitters, showing that high-quality optics plus large atomic sources can suppress phase noise to ~1 mrad (accelerations ~10⁻¹² m·s⁻²).
AI.motivation: Space-based quantum accelerometers are limited by systematic and noise effects; laser wavefront imperfections are a key contributor to interferometer phase bias and fluctuations, and their quantitative impact under microgravity-relevant configurations remains insufficiently characterized.
AI.method: Characterization of phase and intensity fluctuations of the laser beam via power spectral densities, combined with numerical simulations using randomly drawn laser profiles and analytical treatments, averaging the phase response over all atomic trajectories. The sensor modeled uses a low ballistic expansion source of delta-kick collimated Bose-Einstein condensates and Raman double-diffraction beamsplitters suited to microgravity.
AI.result: Laser beam profile inhomogeneities contribute to interferometer phase bias and fluctuations; their magnitude can be reduced to the order of 1 mrad, corresponding to accelerations in the low 10⁻¹² m·s⁻² range, when high-quality optics (of the type used in gravitational wave detectors) are combined with large initial-size atomic sources.
AI.conclusion: Achieving sub-mrad-level phase stability in a space quantum accelerometer requires both high-quality laser optics and large atomic sources, which together enable acceleration sensitivity at the 10⁻¹² m·s⁻² level, providing design guidance for future space-based quantum sensing missions.

title: SI-Traceable Calibration and Performance Benchmarking of a Terahertz Photomixer Transmitter-Receiver System Using a Rydberg Atomic Sensor
summary: Accurate calibration of electromagnetic field strength in the terahertz (THz) frequency regime remains challenging due to the limited availability of SI-traceable field sensors. Here we demonstrate SI-traceable calibration and performance benchmarking of a commercial photomixer-based THz transmitter-receiver system operating near 204 GHz using Rydberg electric-field sensing in a thermal atomic vapor. The THz electric field is extracted from the Autler-Townes (AT) effect of the cesium $17D_{5/2}\rightarrow18P_{3/2}$ Rydberg transition. We measure the strength of AT-split lines as a function of THz detuning from resonance to find the on-resonant Rabi frequency, which, together with atomic transition dipole moments and fundamental constants, yields the THz electric field. The atomically measured field calibrates the photomixer transmitter field and power, while simultaneous measurements with a commercial InGaAs photomixer receiver calibrate the receiver's current-to-field responsivity and convert its current-noise floor into an absolute noise-equivalent THz electric-field sensitivity. Our study demonstrates that Rydberg atomic sensors provide a practical method for SI-traceable calibration and benchmarking of THz transmitter and receiver systems, and for the establishment of a quantitative link between state-of-the-art and absolute atom-based THz sensors.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates SI-traceable calibration of a commercial 204 GHz photomixer-based THz transmitter-receiver system using Rydberg atom-based electric-field sensing in cesium vapor, extracting the field from the Autler-Townes effect and benchmarking both transmitter power and receiver responsivity.
AI.motivation: Accurate calibration of electromagnetic field strength in the THz regime is challenging because SI-traceable field sensors are scarce, limiting reliable benchmarking of THz transmitter and receiver systems.
AI.method: The THz electric field is extracted from the Autler-Townes (AT) splitting of the cesium 17D5/2 → 18P3/2 Rydberg transition. AT-split line strengths are measured as a function of THz detuning from resonance to determine the on-resonant Rabi frequency, which—combined with atomic transition dipole moments and fundamental constants—yields the THz electric field. This atomically measured field calibrates the photomixer transmitter field and power, while simultaneous measurements with a commercial InGaAs photomixer receiver calibrate its current-to-field responsivity and convert its current-noise floor into an absolute noise-equivalent THz electric-field sensitivity.
AI.result: The atomically measured field provides SI-traceable calibration of the photomixer transmitter field and power, and calibrates the commercial InGaAs photomixer receiver's current-to-field responsivity, enabling conversion of its current-noise floor into an absolute noise-equivalent THz electric-field sensitivity near 204 GHz.
AI.conclusion: Rydberg atomic sensors offer a practical method for SI-traceable calibration and benchmarking of THz transmitter and receiver systems, and establish a quantitative link between state-of-the-art and absolute atom-based THz sensors.

title: Optically induced metallic state with persistent monoclinic symmetry in NdNiO$_3$
summary: Understanding whether electronic and structural order remain coupled under nonequilibrium conditions is a central challenge in correlated materials. Here, we simultaneously track metallicity and symmetry across the photoinduced insulator-to-metal transition in NdNiO$_3$ using time-resolved optical reflectivity and symmetry-sensitive second-harmonic generation. We find that metallic reflectivity emerges at significantly lower excitation fluence than restoration of the orthorhombic high-temperature symmetry. As a result, optical excitation stabilizes a metastable state that combines the reflectivity of the metallic phase with the monoclinic symmetry of the insulating phase, revealing an optically induced monoclinic metal. Only at substantially higher fluences does the symmetry fully recover to that of the high-temperature phase. These results demonstrate a nonequilibrium decoupling of metallicity and structural symmetry and establish simultaneous multiprobe spectroscopy as a powerful approach for identifying emergent phases in correlated materials.

AI.tldr: Photoexcitation of NdNiO₃ reveals a metastable monoclinic metal, showing that metallicity and structural symmetry decouple under nonequilibrium conditions.
AI.motivation: Whether electronic and structural order remain coupled under nonequilibrium conditions is a central open question in correlated materials, and resolving it requires simultaneous tracking of both electronic and structural order parameters.
AI.method: Time-resolved optical reflectivity (to track metallicity) combined with symmetry-sensitive second-harmonic generation (to track structural symmetry) were applied simultaneously across the photoinduced insulator-to-metal transition in NdNiO₃.
AI.result: Metallic reflectivity emerges at significantly lower excitation fluence than the restoration of orthorhombic high-temperature symmetry. This stabilizes a metastable state with metallic reflectivity but monoclinic (insulating-phase) symmetry—an optically induced monoclinic metal. Full symmetry recovery to the high-temperature phase occurs only at substantially higher fluences.
AI.conclusion: Metallicity and structural symmetry become decoupled under nonequilibrium photoexcitation, and simultaneous multiprobe spectroscopy is a powerful approach for identifying emergent phases in correlated materials.

title: Instabilities in self-consistent diagrammatic approaches and how to cure them
summary: While self-consistent diagrammatic approaches are widely used to compute the physical properties of correlated quantum materials, their applicability may get severely hindered precisely in the parameter regions, where the most exciting physics is observed. One of the major issues, referred to as "misleading convergence", is the tendency of iterative schemes to converge to unphysical fixed points for intermediate-to-strong electronic interactions, regardless of numerical accuracy of the computation. Here, we explicitly verify that the origin of this problem in several established self-consistent many-electron approaches, defined in the general diagrammatic framework of the boson-exchange formalism, resides exclusively in the stability condition of the respective iteration schemes, and not in an intrinsic breakdown of their self-consistent diagrammatic description. This insight enables a simple and general remedy, as recently proposed in Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 016502 (2026): The redefinition of the iterative procedure, by inverting the unstable eigendirections of the Jacobian associated to the fixed point of the self-consistent algorithm. We illustrate the successful outcome of this procedure by means of systematic calculations performed on testbed, exactly solvable, models. Our results demonstrate that the physical fixed point of the diagrammatic schemes we considered can be stabilized, de facto, across the entire parameter range, including the most challenging nonperturbative/strong-coupling regimes.

AI.tldr: The "misleading convergence" of self-consistent diagrammatic many-electron schemes arises from unstable iteration fixed points rather than a breakdown of the underlying diagrammatic description; inverting the unstable eigendirections of the Jacobian restores the physical fixed point across all coupling regimes.
AI.motivation: Self-consistent diagrammatic methods are standard for correlated quantum materials, but their reliability degrades precisely in the intermediate-to-strong coupling regions where the most interesting physics appears. Iterative schemes can converge to unphysical fixed points—an issue known as "misleading convergence"—independent of numerical precision. The paper aims to identify the true origin of this failure and to validate a general remedy.
AI.method: The authors analyze several established self-consistent many-electron approaches formulated within the general boson-exchange diagrammatic framework. They demonstrate that the misleading convergence stems exclusively from the stability condition of the iteration schemes, not from an intrinsic failure of the self-consistent diagrammatic description. They then apply a remedy proposed in Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 016502 (2026): redefining the iterative procedure by inverting the unstable eigendirections of the Jacobian associated with the fixed point of the self-consistent algorithm. Systematic calculations are performed on testbed, exactly solvable models.
AI.result: The analysis confirms that the unphysical fixed points originate from the stability properties of the iteration, and the Jacobian-inversion procedure successfully stabilizes the physical fixed point. Calculations on exactly solvable testbed models show the remedy works de facto across the entire parameter range, including the most challenging nonperturbative/strong-coupling regimes.
AI.conclusion: Misleading convergence in self-consistent diagrammatic schemes is a purely algorithmic stability problem, not an intrinsic limitation of the diagrammatic description. Inverting the unstable Jacobian eigendirections provides a simple, general cure that stabilizes the physical fixed point for intermediate-to-strong electronic interactions, extending the applicability of these methods into the nonperturbative regime.

title: A model of grain growth in UN integrating molecular dynamics, phase-field modeling, and uncertainty quantification
summary: Grain growth kinetics and grain-boundary (GB) properties in uranium mononitride (UN) are investigated through an integrated multiscale framework combining molecular dynamics (MD), phase-field modeling, and surrogate-assisted uncertainty quantification. MD simulations yield GB energies for 27 symmetric tilt boundaries from 0--2000~K, which are consistent with available DFT values. The average GB energy is nearly temperature-independent below 1000~K and increases at higher temperatures. A mechanistic pore-drag model applied to the only available grain growth dataset for actinide nitrides yields a mobility reduction factor of $s \approx 0.93$--$0.99$, statistically indistinguishable from unity, confirming that pore drag is negligible under the experimental conditions. The intrinsic GB mobility is therefore extracted directly from the effective mobility, yielding $M_0 = 2.05\times10^{-15}$~m$^4$/(J$\cdot$s) and $Q_M = 0.89$~eV. Phase-field simulations conducted from 1500--2000~K confirm normal curvature-driven grain growth, with grain size distributions converging to the Hillert-like form. A surrogate-assisted global sensitivity analysis---combining principal component analysis, Gaussian process regression, and Sobol decomposition---reveals that the mobility prefactor $M_0$ dominates output variance at all times, followed by the activation energy $Q_M$, while the GB energy $γ$ contributes minimally. These results establish the first quantitative grain growth framework for UN and identify the reduction of uncertainty in $M_0$ and $Q_M$ as the highest-priority target for future experimental efforts.

AI.tldr: An integrated MD + phase-field + surrogate-assisted UQ framework characterizes grain growth kinetics and GB properties in UN, showing negligible pore drag and identifying mobility prefactor and activation energy as the dominant variance sources.
AI.motivation: Grain growth kinetics and grain-boundary properties in uranium mononitride (UN) are poorly quantified experimentally, and the limited grain growth dataset for actinide nitrides leaves open questions about the role of pore drag and which parameters control microstructural evolution.
AI.method: Molecular dynamics simulations compute GB energies for 27 symmetric tilt boundaries from 0–2000 K, giving temperature-dependent GB energies. A mechanistic pore-drag model is applied to the sole actinide nitride grain growth dataset to extract a mobility reduction factor s. Intrinsic GB mobility is extracted from effective mobility, and phase-field simulations (1500–2000 K) model curvature-driven grain growth. A surrogate-assisted global sensitivity analysis combines principal component analysis, Gaussian process regression, and Sobol decomposition.
AI.result: MD GB energies agree with available DFT values; average GB energy is nearly temperature-independent below 1000 K and rises above it. The pore-drag model gives s ≈ 0.93–0.99, statistically indistinguishable from unity, indicating negligible pore drag. Intrinsic mobility yields M0 = 2.05×10⁻¹⁵ m⁴/(J·s) and QM = 0.89 eV. Phase-field simulations confirm normal curvature-driven growth with grain size distributions converging to a Hillert-like form. Sensitivity analysis shows M0 dominates output variance at all times, followed by QM, with γ contributing minimally.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes the first quantitative grain growth framework for UN and identifies reducing uncertainty in M0 and QM as the highest-priority target for future experimental efforts.

title: A substrate booster for P-type 2D ferromagnetic semiconductor
summary: Spin transistors with its both charge and spin properties tuned via electrostatic gating are believed capable for widespread use, which however have proven challenging due to the extreme rareness of their physical base -- magnetic semiconductors. The latter are limited within very few systems including diluted magnetic semiconductors (DMS) and two-dimensional ferromagnetic semiconductors (2D-FMS), and known to suffer from inadequate gate-tunability of their electric and/or magnetic properties. Here, we show a substrate engineering paradigm by interfacing few-layered Cr$_{2}$Ge$_{2}$Te$_{6}$ (FL-CGT) with an antiferromagnetic insulator CrOCl. Owing to the subtle interfacial charge transfer couplings, CGT can be drastically turned from an ambipolar semiconductor into a high performance P-type semiconductor. When cooled below the Curie temperature, the ON-OFF ratio in such substrate-boosted FMS field-effect transistor (FET) reaches 10$^{5}$ with its coercive field $H_{c}$ of magnetic hysteresis loop tunable by a factor of more than 200$\%$, enabling {gate-assisted magnetic switching in the prototype semiconducting spin transistor architecture}. A crossover from critical power-law scaling to a dual power-law behaviour under heavy hole doping was further observed. Our findings {signify} an efficient interfacial charge transfer and electrically modulated magnetic anisotropy energy supported by calculations. This high performance P-type FMS-FET system suggests that active substrate-boosting paradigm might be a powerful path for the investigation of future gate-tunable spintronic devices.

AI.tldr: Substrate engineering (interfacing FL-Cr2Ge2Te6 with antiferromagnetic insulator CrOCl) converts an ambipolar semiconductor into a high-performance P-type ferromagnetic semiconductor FET with gate-tunable magnetism, enabling gate-assisted magnetic switching for spintronic devices.
AI.motivation: Spin transistors require magnetic semiconductors whose electric and magnetic properties can be electrostatically tuned, but such materials are extremely rare (limited to DMS and 2D-FMS) and typically suffer from inadequate gate-tunability of their electric and/or magnetic properties.
AI.method: A substrate engineering paradigm is introduced by interfacing few-layered Cr2Ge2Te6 (FL-CGT) with an antiferromagnetic insulator CrOCl. Interfacial charge transfer coupling is exploited, supported by calculations, to modulate the semiconductor behavior and magnetic anisotropy energy.
AI.result: Subtle interfacial charge transfer drastically converts CGT from an ambipolar semiconductor into a high-performance P-type semiconductor. Below the Curie temperature, the ON-OFF ratio of the substrate-boosted FMS FET reaches 10^5, and the coercive field Hc is tunable by more than 200%, enabling gate-assisted magnetic switching. A crossover from critical power-law scaling to dual power-law behavior appears under heavy hole doping.
AI.conclusion: The interfacial charge transfer and electrically modulated magnetic anisotropy energy are confirmed by calculations. The high-performance P-type FMS-FET system suggests that active substrate-boosting is a powerful path toward future gate-tunable spintronic devices.

title: Block entropy area based non-local fermionic mode optimization with gradient disentanglers
summary: We introduce a systematic block entropy area based mode optimization algorithm for many-body quantum states of interacting fermions represented by matrix product states. From the gradient of a global cost function, the block entropy area, a long-ranged, non-interacting effective disentangler Hamiltonian is formed. We then simulate the time-dependent Schrödinger equation driven by the disentangler Hamiltonian by employing the time-dependent variational principle based on projector splitting, and minimize the cost function. The combination of the density matrix renormalization group with this gradient-based entanglement minimization forms an efficient low-rank iterative ground-state algorithm that also provides an optimized single-particle basis for matrix product state representation. We demonstrate the method on two-dimensional lattice models of interacting fermions and the Fe${_4}$S${_4}$ cluster, and show its robustness and superiority over earlier protocols using nearest-neighbor mode rotations and reorderings.

AI.tldr: Introduces a block entropy area based mode optimization algorithm that combines DMRG with gradient-based entanglement minimization (via a disentangler Hamiltonian and TDVP) to efficiently find low-rank ground states and optimized single-particle bases for interacting fermions.
AI.motivation: Matrix product state representations of interacting fermion systems are limited by entanglement growth. Earlier mode optimization protocols relied on nearest-neighbor mode rotations and reorderings, which are local and thus insufficient to reduce long-range entanglement. A more global, systematic mode optimization is needed to lower the bond dimension and improve efficiency.
AI.method: The algorithm optimizes modes using a global cost function, the block entropy area. From its gradient, a long-ranged, non-interacting effective disentangler Hamiltonian is constructed. The time-dependent Schrödinger equation under this disentangler Hamiltonian is simulated with the time-dependent variational principle based on projector splitting to minimize the cost function. This gradient-based entanglement minimization is combined with the density matrix renormalization group, yielding an iterative low-rank ground-state algorithm that simultaneously produces an optimized single-particle basis for the MPS representation.
AI.result: The method is demonstrated on two-dimensional lattice models of interacting fermions and the Fe4S4 cluster. It proves robust and outperforms earlier protocols that use nearest-neighbor mode rotations and reorderings.
AI.conclusion: A systematic, gradient-based mode optimization scheme using the block entropy area cost function and a disentangler Hamiltonian, integrated with DMRG and TDVP, provides an efficient low-rank ground-state algorithm with an optimized single-particle basis, superior to prior local mode-rotation approaches.

title: Nondipole Coulomb effects in strong x-ray field ionization
summary: Atomic ionization in superintense x-ray fields is studied through numerical solutions of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation including nondipole corrections. The role of the Coulomb potential of the atomic core in the nondipole regime is analyzed for a linearly polarized laser field. In the considered high-frequency and high-intensity stabilization regime, the photoelectron spectra are dominated by a near-zero-energy structure, while above-threshold ionization peaks are suppressed. Two sub-regimes in the nondipole case are identified based on the scaling of the Coulomb momentum transfer, when the Coulomb effect during the interaction with the laser field is either significant or minor. The Coulomb influenced regime sets in within the realm of relatively low field strengths, high laser frequencies, and long pulse durations. An intuitive model explaining the distinct features in the photoelectron momentum distributions and the Coulomb effect scaling is provided.

AI.tldr: Nondipole effects in superintense x-ray atomic ionization are studied via the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, revealing a Coulomb-dominated regime and a Coulomb-minor regime distinguished by Coulomb momentum transfer scaling, with photoelectron spectra dominated by a near-zero-energy structure.
AI.motivation: To understand how the atomic core Coulomb potential influences ionization in the nondipole regime of superintense, high-frequency x-ray fields, and to identify the conditions under which the Coulomb effect becomes significant.
AI.method: Numerical solution of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation including nondipole (magnetic-field) corrections for a linearly polarized laser field, combined with an intuitive analytical model.
AI.result: In the high-frequency, high-intensity stabilization regime, photoelectron spectra are dominated by a near-zero-energy structure while above-threshold ionization peaks are suppressed. Two nondipole sub-regimes are identified based on the scaling of the Coulomb momentum transfer: a Coulomb-influenced regime, occurring at relatively low field strengths, high frequencies, and long pulse durations, and a Coulomb-minor regime.
AI.conclusion: The Coulomb effect in the nondipole regime can be either significant or minor depending on the scaling of the Coulomb momentum transfer, and the proposed intuitive model accounts for the distinct features in the photoelectron momentum distributions and the Coulomb effect scaling.

title: A Community-Developed Domain Ontology for Magnetic Materials
summary: Magnetic materials play a crucial role in energy-related technologies, mobility, and sensing, but their complex multiscale behaviour and the coexistence of multiple unit systems pose persistent challenges for data exchange and interpretation. This paper presents a domain ontology for magnetic materials, developed within the European Union funded Magnetic Multiscale Modelling Suite (MaMMoS) project and aligned with the Elementary Multiperspective Material Ontology (EMMO). The ontology formalises intrinsic, hysteretic, and microstructural properties across multiple length scales and supports semantic interoperability between simulation tools, databases, and experimental workflows. One key feature of the ontology is its code-based and human-readable structure, enabled through the EMMOntoPy framework, which allows for direct manipulation and versioning without relying on opaque .owl or .ttl files. This facilitates collaborative development and improves transparency. The ontology supports FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles and is openly available for extension by the community. The aim of the MaMMoS project is to foster reproducibility, improve traceability, and promote the adoption of ontology in the magnetism domain. The ontology that has been developed already serves as the foundation for multiple software tools that handle all kinds of magnetic material data.

AI.tldr: A domain ontology for magnetic materials, developed in the EU-funded MaMMoS project and aligned with EMMO, formalizes multiscale magnetic properties in a code-based, human-readable format to enable semantic interoperability and FAIR data practices in magnetism research.
AI.motivation: Magnetic materials are central to energy, mobility, and sensing technologies, yet their complex multiscale behaviour and the coexistence of multiple unit systems hinder data exchange and interpretation. There is a need for a shared semantic framework to unify simulation, database, and experimental data.
AI.method: The authors developed a domain ontology for magnetic materials within the MaMMoS project, aligned with the Elementary Multiperspective Material Ontology (EMMO). It formalizes intrinsic, hysteretic, and microstructural properties across multiple length scales, and is implemented via the EMMOntoPy framework, giving a code-based, human-readable structure that supports versioning without opaque .owl or .ttl files.
AI.result: The ontology supports semantic interoperability between simulation tools, databases, and experimental workflows, adheres to FAIR principles, and is openly available for community extension. It already serves as the foundation for multiple software tools handling magnetic material data.
AI.conclusion: The MaMMoS ontology aims to foster reproducibility, improve traceability, and promote ontology adoption in the magnetism domain, offering a transparent, collaborative, and extensible basis for managing magnetic material data.

title: Silicon Solar Cell Design for >30% Efficiency via Singlet Fission
summary: Singlet fission (SF) materials convert high-energy photons into multiple charge carriers, providing a route to exceed the efficiency limits of single-junction silicon solar cells without many of the complexities of multi-junction tandem designs. Following the first demonstration of an SF-enhanced silicon solar cell in 2025, there is a need to understand how SF materials can be effectively integrated into high-efficiency industrial silicon devices and translated from proof of concept to a manufacturable technology. Using coupled optical and electrical simulations, we assess the efficiency potential of several industrially relevant silicon cell architectures combined with SF materials. Interdigitated back-contact (IBC) cells offer the greatest potential for improvement due to unrestricted front-surface access and can achieve efficiencies exceeding 33%. However, performance is highly sensitive to front-surface passivation quality. Appropriate silicon design, particularly controlled surface doping and fixed interfacial charge, can mitigate recombination losses and relax passivation requirements for ultra-thin exciton-transfer layers.

AI.tldr: Coupled optical-electrical simulations show that integrating singlet fission materials with industrial silicon architectures—especially IBC cells—can exceed 33% efficiency, though performance hinges on front-surface passivation quality and interfacial design.
AI.motivation: Singlet fission (SF) materials can convert high-energy photons into multiple charge carriers, offering a path to surpass single-junction silicon solar cell efficiency limits without multi-junction tandem complexity. Following the first SF-enhanced silicon solar cell demonstration in 2025, there is a need to understand effective integration of SF materials into high-efficiency industrial silicon devices and their translation from proof of concept to manufacturable technology.
AI.method: The study uses coupled optical and electrical simulations to assess the efficiency potential of several industrially relevant silicon cell architectures combined with SF materials, evaluating integration and loss mechanisms.
AI.result: Interdigitated back-contact (IBC) cells show the greatest improvement potential due to unrestricted front-surface access, achieving efficiencies exceeding 33%. Performance is highly sensitive to front-surface passivation quality, and appropriate silicon design—particularly controlled surface doping and fixed interfacial charge—can mitigate recombination losses and relax passivation requirements for ultra-thin exciton-transfer layers.
AI.conclusion: SF materials can be effectively integrated into high-efficiency industrial silicon devices, with IBC architectures offering the highest efficiency gains. However, realizing this potential requires careful silicon design and passivation engineering to manage front-surface recombination and enable manufacturable SF-enhanced cells.

title: Vacancy Order and Physical Properties of a Ternary Compound Fe0.68Pd0.80Te with an α-Fe1+xTe-Type Structure
summary: We report the identification and characterization of a new compound Fe0.68Pd0.80Te with an α-Fe1+xTe prototype structure. Different from the Fe-square net and minor occupancy of interstitial Fe-sites in Fe1+xTe, Fe0.68Pd0.80Te is featured by a Pdsquare net and near 68% occupancy of the corresponding interstitial Fe-sites. Furthermore, noncontact atomic force microscopy and X-ray diffraction provide evidence for the existence of a 3*3*3 Pd-vacancy order in this layered material. A spin-glass ground state below Tg 40 K is identified via magnetic characterization. Electrical transport measurements show that Fe0.68Pd0.80Te is a semiconductor with a very small band gap below 10 meV. It has weak negative magnetoresistance and holelike charge carriers below room temperature. Our results demonstrate its potentials for further exploring various quantum phenomena.

Transport shows semiconducting behavior with a very small band gap below 10 meV, weak negative magnetoresistance, and holelike carriers below room temperature.

title: In-plane magnetic field control of anomalous Hall response enabled by magnetic anisotropy engineering
summary: Engineering magnetic anisotropy provides a powerful route to control magnetization orientation and unlock emerging functionalities in opto-spintronic and current-driven devices. Beyond its role in magnetization reversal, the effective anisotropy can strongly influence the magnetotransport response, offering an additional degree of freedom to tune new device functionalities. In this work, we report a magnetotransport study of a ferrimagnetic [Tb/Co]$_{\times 5}$ multilayer grown with a Tb thickness gradient, whose wedge-shaped tilts the uniaxial anisotropy axis slightly away from the film normal. Anomalous Hall resistivity measurements from 80 K to 300 K reveal a spin reorientation transition, while the angular dependence of the magnetotransport responses exposes the crucial role of the tilted anisotropy. A simplified macrospin model reproduces the full angular response across the transition and shows that the observed anomalous Hall effect when the in-plane magnetic field is applied originates from the tilt of the uniaxial anisotropy axis, which supplies a built-in symmetry-breaking mechanism, enabling in-plane field control over the out-of-plane anomalous Hall response, sign included. These findings establish tilted magnetic anisotropy as a promising route toward Hall effect-based sensor applications and highlight Tb/Co multilayers as a versatile platform for anisotropy-engineered spintronic devices.

They measure anomalous Hall resistivity from 80 K to 300 K and analyze the angular dependence of the magnetotransport responses. A simplified macrospin model is used to reproduce the full angular response across the transition.

The angular dependence of the magnetotransport responses exposes the crucial role of the tilted anisotropy. The macrospin model reproduces the full angular response across the transition and shows that the observed anomalous Hall effect under an in-plane magnetic field originates from the tilt of the uniaxial anisotropy axis, which supplies a built-in symmetry-breaking mechanism.
